ClickFix Campaign Uses EtherHiding and GULoader to Infect Windows Users via Fake CAPTCHA

Cyber Security News
2026-06-17 4 use cases 1 technique 4 kill-chain phases detected

A new cyberattack campaign is targeting Windows users through fake CAPTCHA pages, combining three techniques to slip past standard security defenses without raising alarms. The campaign, first observed in April 2026, begins on a compromised European small-business website and ends with an attempt to load GULoader, a memory-based malware downloader, onto a victim&#8217;s machine. Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("172a25a9ed8b798d8baeec29424b46627b5b39723b37c787f928d3700509001e", "236e1bef618edfe7f7c29ee2b4cba620") or SHA1 in~ ("172a25a9ed8b798d8baeec29424b46627b5b39723b37c787f928d3700509001e", "236e1bef618edfe7f7c29ee2b4cba620") or MD5 in~ ("172a25a9ed8b798d8baeec29424b46627b5b39723b37c787f928d3700509001e", "236e1bef618edfe7f7c29ee2b4cba620")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("172a25a9ed8b798d8baeec29424b46627b5b39723b37c787f928d3700509001e", "236e1bef618edfe7f7c29ee2b4cba620") or SHA1 in~ ("172a25a9ed8b798d8baeec29424b46627b5b39723b37c787f928d3700509001e", "236e1bef618edfe7f7c29ee2b4cba620") or MD5 in~ ("172a25a9ed8b798d8baeec29424b46627b5b39723b37c787f928d3700509001e", "236e1bef618edfe7f7c29ee2b4cba620")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["172a25a9ed8b798d8baeec29424b46627b5b39723b37c787f928d3700509001e", "236e1bef618edfe7f7c29ee2b4cba620"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| sort - click_time

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Rclone rcd / --rc-serve running without RC authentication (CVE-2026-49980 exposure) · [LLM] Vulnerable rclone versions present in the fleet (CVE-2026-49980 inventory) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Browser process connecting to localhost rclone rc port (CVE-2026-49980 cross-site exploitation)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Rclone spawning shell / interpreter child process (CVE-2026-49980 post-exploitation)
Rclone rcd / --rc-serve running without RC authentication (CVE-2026-49980 exposure) AIReconnaissance High
Hunts for rclone processes started with rcd or --rc-serve but without any of --rc-user / --rc-pass / --rc-htpasswd / --rc-no-auth-override. Per the advisory, this is the exact precondition for unauthenticated command execution via inline remote instantiation. Surfaces exposed hosts before exploitation, not after. Rationale: Targets the literal preconditions named in the GHSA: '--rc-serve flag must be in use' and 'deployed without global RC HTTP authentication - so not using --rc-user/--rc-pass/--rc-htpasswd'. Detects the exposed surface before exploitation, so high signal even without active attack. Cross-checked with rclone forum 1.74.3 release notes and the linked sister advisory GHSA-jfwf-28xr-xw6q. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/rclone/rclone/security/advisories/GHSA-jfwf-28xr-xw6q • https://forum.rclone.org/t/rclone-release-1-74-3/53880 • https://ccb.belgium.be/advisories/warning-two-critical-unauthenticated-code-execution-vulnerabilities-rclone-patch
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup admin running 'rclone rcd' on a kiosk-only host for local-only sync testing
  • CI job that briefly launches 'rclone rcd' for an integration test with the default localhost binding
  • Self-hosted personal cloud setup where the user wraps auth at the reverse-proxy layer (e.g. Caddy/Traefik basic-auth in front of rcd)
  • Developer running 'rclone rcd --rc-no-auth' explicitly (still vulnerable; this is a TP, not an FP)
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--rc-addr 127.0.0.1", "--rc-addr localhost", "--rc-addr ::1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm rclone version with 'rclone version' on the host — versions >=1.55.0 and <=1.74.2 are RCE-vulnerable; 1.46.0-1.54.x are file-read only. Identify the listening interface ('netstat -lnp | grep rclone' or 'Get-NetTCPConnection -OwningProcess <pid>'); a non-loopback bind is a critical exposure. 2) Contain: stop the rclone rcd process; if business need exists, restart with --rc-user/--rc-pass or upgrade to 1.74.3 before re-enabling. Block inbound TCP/5572 (or custom --rc-addr port) at host firewall until patched. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'rclone spawning shell children' on the same DeviceId for the last 30d to confirm no prior exploitation, and check DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for CveId 'CVE-2026-49980' across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "rclone.exe" or FileName =~ "rclone"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--rc-serve", " rcd ", " rcd")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--rc" and not(ProcessCommandLine has "--rc-"))
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--rc-user", "--rc-pass", "--rc-htpasswd"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\rclone.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/rclone"

Rclone spawning shell / interpreter child process (CVE-2026-49980 post-exploitation) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for the rclone process spawning cmd.exe / powershell.exe / sh / bash / curl / certutil / wscript and similar LOLBins. Under normal use rclone never spawns shells; this child set on an rclone parent is the direct fingerprint of inline-remote command-execution payloads (e.g. webdav bearer_token_command='/usr/bin/touch ...') landing on the host. Rationale: Rclone is a Go binary whose entire purpose is moving bytes between cloud backends - it has no legitimate workflow that spawns interpreters or LOLBins. The CCB Belgium advisory and security-online write-up both confirm the exploit payload is delivered through inline-remote backend options that fork a child shell (canonical PoC uses webdav `bearer_token_command='/usr/bin/touch /tmp/...'`). This child-process shape is the cleanest possible exploitation fingerprint and survives URL/payload obfuscation. Cross-checked against: • https://ccb.belgium.be/advisories/warning-two-critical-unauthenticated-code-execution-vulnerabilities-rclone-patch • https://securityonline.info/rclone-command-execution/ • https://github.com/rclone/rclone/security/advisories/GHSA-jfwf-28xr-xw6q
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user-written wrapper script that pipes rclone output through 'sh -c' (rare; usually visible by a single repeating cmdline)
  • Rclone --script-config or hook-style integrations where an operator wires post-sync shell hooks
  • Backup orchestration tools that exec rclone then pipe rclone-printed manifests into curl/wget for notification webhooks (parent will usually be the orchestrator, not rclone itself)
  • QA/test harness firing rclone with debug wrappers
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ParentCmd of the rclone process — if it contains 'rcd', '--rc-serve', or '--rc', treat as confirmed CVE-2026-49980 exploitation. Capture ChildCmd: the executed command is the attacker's payload (touch markers, reverse shells, miner installs, cred dumpers). 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response or Falcon RTR; kill the rclone rcd process; rotate any credentials, cloud tokens, and rclone.conf entries the rclone process user had access to (rclone.conf typically holds long-lived backend tokens — assume them burnt). 3) Hunt: pivot on the rclone process user across DeviceLogonEvents, AADSignInEventsBeta, and CloudAppEvents for the last 30 days; search DeviceNetworkEvents from the same host for outbound to attacker-controlled WebDAV URLs (the inline-remote vector frequently chains to webdav backends).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "rclone.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "rclone"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","sh","bash","zsh","dash","ksh","tcsh","python","python3","perl","ruby","node","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentFile = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd  = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildFile  = FileName,
          ChildCmd   = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildPath  = FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\rclone.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "/rclone"
| extend ChildBin = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| extend ChildBinNix = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "/")[-1])
| where ChildBin in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
   or ChildBinNix in~ ("sh","bash","zsh","dash","ksh","tcsh","python","python3","perl","ruby","node","nc","ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable rclone versions present in the fleet (CVE-2026-49980 inventory) AIReconnaissance High
Inventory hunt to enumerate every host running rclone 1.46.0-1.74.2 so the team can prioritise patching to 1.74.3+. Critical companion to the exploitation detections because the GHSA gives a clean version-range cutoff, and unlike the runtime detections this surfaces dormant exposure (rclone installed but not currently running rcd). Rationale: GHSA-qw24-gh76-8rvv gives a precise affected-version window ('>= 1.46.0, <= 1.74.2' with command-execution path opening at 1.55.0). Defender TVM already maps published CVEs to inventory so CveId='CVE-2026-49980' is the cleanest single predicate; Falcon doesn't ship a CVE→inventory join so we fall back to regex on the rclone binary's FileVersion to cover the same range. Cross-referenced with the rclone forum 1.74.3 release notes and Softpedia version history. Cross-checked against: • https://forum.rclone.org/t/rclone-release-1-74-3/53880 • https://www.softpedia.com/get/Internet/File-Sharing/Rclone.shtml
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped or isolated VMs where the version is vulnerable but the rc API is genuinely never started (still worth patching — partial FP)
  • Containers where rclone is bundled inside an image but the running entrypoint never invokes rcd (true exposure only if the container image gets re-purposed)
  • rclone shipped inside a third-party application's installer (e.g. NAS-vendor sync app) — patching path is via the vendor, not direct upgrade
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank the hits by IsInternetFacing=true and by hosts that match UC1's rcd-without-auth detection — those are immediate patch targets. 2) Contain: queue an emergency patch ring for rclone >=1.74.3 via the existing patch tooling (Intune/SCCM/Ansible). For hosts that cannot patch within 24h, push a host-firewall rule blocking inbound to TCP/5572 and any custom --rc-addr port. 3) Hunt: for every vulnerable host, run a 30-day retro-hunt of UC2 ('rclone spawning shell children') to verify no prior exploitation went unnoticed. Cross-check DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities for the sister CVE GHSA-jfwf-28xr-xw6q (operations/fsinfo variant) which has the same patched-version cutoff.

Browser process connecting to localhost rclone rc port (CVE-2026-49980 cross-site exploitation) AIExploitation Medium
The advisory specifically calls out that a public HTTPS page with an <img> tag pointing at http://127.0.0.1:5572/[remote:...]/file can trigger the payload against a localhost-only rclone rcd. Browsers do not normally connect to TCP/5572; a browser→loopback:5572 connection is therefore a strong signal of an in-progress cross-site attack against a developer/admin workstation. Rationale: Pulled directly from the advisory's 'Additional impact' section: 'Firefox triggered the payload from a public HTTPS page containing only an <img> tag pointing at http://127.0.0.1:5572/...'. Port 5572 is the documented rclone rcd default. Browser→loopback:5572 is otherwise vanishingly rare so the FP floor is essentially zero except where a developer is hand-driving the rclone web UI. Cross-checked against securityonline.info and the CCB advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://securityonline.info/rclone-command-execution/ • https://ccb.belgium.be/advisories/warning-two-critical-unauthenticated-code-execution-vulnerabilities-rclone-patch
ATT&CKT1190 T1185
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer manually browsing the rclone WebUI at http://127.0.0.1:5572/ (usually a single sustained session, not a single drive-by image fetch)
  • A locally-installed self-hosted UI bookmarked by an admin
  • Browser-based health-check extensions that periodically probe localhost ports
  • Penetration testing tools or vulnerability scanners (Burp, ZAP) running on the same host and intentionally walking localhost ports
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--app=http://127.0.0.1:5572"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the originating tab/URL — Defender DeviceEvents and browser history will show the referer page that contained the <img> tag. A single drive-by hit from an unfamiliar domain is the smoking gun; a sustained session with multiple endpoints is likely the operator's own use of the rclone WebUI. 2) Contain: terminate the rclone rcd process on the host, block the originating domain at the proxy, and force-close the browser tabs on the affected user. If exploitation likely succeeded (corroborated by UC2 child-process hit within ±30s), isolate the host. 3) Hunt: search EmailUrlInfo, UrlClickEvents, and the proxy for the originating domain across the org; pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for any other host that connected to the same external referer in the last 7 days — the malicious page may have targeted a population of rclone users.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 5572
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1", "0.0.0.0")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("firefox.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","iexplore.exe","safari.exe","arc.exe","librewolf.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 5572
| where DestinationIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
   or (isnotempty(RequestURL) and RequestURL has_any ("127.0.0.1:5572", "localhost:5572", "[::1]:5572"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP,
          DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LiteLLM proxy Host header injection auth bypass (CVE-2026-49468) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to LiteLLM proxy management endpoints (/key/*, /user/new, /team/new, /model/info, /spend, /customer/new) where the Host header contains path/URL metacharacters or otherwise diverges from the proxy's canonical hostname — the precise primitive Le The Thang / Kim Ngoc Chung used to make get_request_route() evaluate a different route than FastAPI dispatched. Focuses on successful 2xx responses against management routes where the Host header looks crafted rather than canonical. Rationale: Detection anchors on the exact vulnerable code path named in the GHSA — get_request_route() in litellm/proxy/auth/auth_utils.py reads the path from a Starlette URL reconstructed from the Host header. We pair (a) the LiteLLM management routes (/key/*, /user/new, /team/new, /model/info, /spend, /global_spend, /customer/new — the actual routes guarded by master_key auth in the proxy code) with (b) Host-header shapes that should never appear in a normal request: URL metachars (/, ?, #, @, \), whitespace, bare IPs, or hostnames not on the org's canonical proxy allowlist. Drops Defender KQL — Defender Advanced Hunting tables (DeviceNetworkEvents, DeviceProcessEvents) don't surface inbound HTTP request headers. Falcon FDR / CloudWatch likewise omit raw Host headers from inbound HTTP traffic in their default schemas. No external sources cross-checked — CVE published 2026 with no public IOCs / PoCs / second-source coverage yet.
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Burp, ZAP) deliberately probing the proxy with malformed Host headers
  • Misconfigured upstream load balancer / Kubernetes ingress forwarding a bare pod-IP in the Host header instead of the canonical FQDN
  • Developers hitting the proxy directly via curl/Postman with Host headers like 'localhost:4000' that don't match the production allowlist
  • Service-mesh sidecars (Istio, Linkerd) rewriting Host to internal cluster DNS names not in the org allowlist
  • Health-check probes from external monitoring (Pingdom, Datadog Synthetics) using the IP literal rather than the FQDN
Suppression filter
| where not(SrcIpAddr in ("10.0.0.0/8"))  // exclude internal scanner range — tune per environment
| where not(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Nessus", "Burp", "ZAP", "Nuclei", "Pingdom", "Datadog Synthetics"))
| where not(HttpHostName matches regex @"^10\.|^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|^192\.168\.")  // drop internal-IP literals from k8s ingress
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pivot on SrcIpAddr / HttpHostName from the hit — is this a known scanner CIDR or service-mesh source? Pull the prior 24h of requests from that source to the LiteLLM proxy; legitimate clients should hit /chat/completions, not /key/* or /user/new. Confirm proxy version with 'pip show litellm' on the host — if < 1.84.0 the bypass is reachable. Step 2 (contain): if the request was successful (2xx) AND the source is unexpected, immediately rotate every master_key and virtual key the proxy issued (LiteLLM admin UI > Keys > regenerate), block the source IP at the upstream WAF/CDN, and upgrade LiteLLM to >= 1.84.0 in the same change window. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on any /key/generate or /user/new 2xx responses in the last 30d from non-allowlisted Host headers; any virtual keys minted that way are attacker-controlled — query downstream LLM-provider logs (OpenAI, Anthropic) for usage tied to those keys.
let LiteLLMHosts = dynamic(["litellm.example.internal", "ai-proxy.example.internal"]);
let AdminRouteRegex = @"(?i)/(key/(generate|info|update|delete|list)|user/(new|info|update|delete)|team/(new|update|info|delete)|model/(new|info|delete)|customer/new|spend|global_spend)";
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(Url)
| where Url matches regex AdminRouteRegex
| where HttpStatusCode startswith "2"
| extend HostLower = tolower(HttpHostName)
| extend HostIsSuspicious = (HostLower matches regex @"[\\/\?#@]")                 // path/URL metachars smuggled into Host
                         or (HostLower matches regex @"^\d{1,3}(\.\d{1,3}){3}(:\d+)?$") // bare IP literal
                         or (HostLower matches regex @"\s")                              // whitespace in Host
                         or (array_length(split(HostLower, ",")) > 1)                     // multiple host values
                         or (isnotempty(HostLower) and not(HostLower in (LiteLLMHosts)))   // unknown host vs canonical allowlist
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpMethod, HttpHostName, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable LiteLLM (< 1.84.0) exposed to network — CVE-2026-49468 inventory AIWeaponization High
Identifies hosts running pip:litellm at a version below 1.84.0, the patched release for CVE-2026-49468. Prioritizes internet-facing devices since the bypass requires that no upstream Host-validating layer (CDN, reverse proxy with server_name allowlist, host-based LB) is in front of the proxy. Rationale: Anchored on the exact patched version named in the GHSA (1.84.0) and the assigned CVE ID (CVE-2026-49468). DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities is the authoritative inventory join because Defender TVM maps CVE → DeviceId directly once the catalog ingests the advisory; the inventory-side fallback (SoftwareName =~ 'litellm' with manual semver comparison) covers the gap before catalog sync. Joining DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing surfaces the exact hosts where the GHSA's caveat 'most deployments are not affected — bypass is blocked by upstream Host validation' breaks down (i.e. internet-exposed proxies without a CDN/WAF). No external IOCs to corroborate (CVE only just published).
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstations with litellm installed locally for testing — not actually running a network-exposed proxy
  • CI/CD build agents with litellm pinned in test dependency manifests
  • Hosts where TVM hasn't refreshed inventory since the litellm upgrade — stale version data
  • Containers / venvs where litellm is bundled but never started as a proxy server
  • Air-gapped lab environments where the proxy is reachable only on loopback
Suppression filter
| where IsInternetFacing == true or DeviceName !has_any ("-dev", "-build", "-ci", "laptop", "workstation")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): for each DeviceId returned, check whether the proxy is actually listening on a network interface — `netstat -lntp | grep -E ':(4000|8000)'` or equivalent — and whether IsInternetFacing=true; prioritize internet-exposed first, internal-listening second, dev-machines last. Step 2 (contain): upgrade to litellm >= 1.84.0 (`pip install --upgrade litellm`); if upgrade is blocked, place the proxy behind a Host-validating layer per the GHSA workaround (Cloudflare/WAF, nginx with explicit server_name, host-based LB rule) before the next maintenance window. Step 3 (hunt): for any host that was internet-facing AND vulnerable, run UC1 (Host-header anomaly hunt) against its access logs for the entire exposure window — assume any /key/* or /user/new 2xx hit during that window may be attacker-issued and rotate the affected master_key and downstream LLM-provider API keys.
let VulnVersion = "1.84.0";
let VulnerableHosts = DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName =~ "litellm" or SoftwareName has "litellm"
| extend Major = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)\.", 1, SoftwareVersion)),
         Minor = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.(\d+)\.", 1, SoftwareVersion)),
         Patch = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| where (Major < 1) or (Major == 1 and Minor < 84) or (Major == 1 and Minor == 84 and Patch < 0)
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform;
VulnerableHosts
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers) by DeviceId
) on DeviceId
| union (
    DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | where CveId == "CVE-2026-49468"
    | project DeviceId, DeviceName, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
)
| project Timestamp = now(), DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc

Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin install by ID (Aikido campaign) AIInstallation High
Hunts for installation of the 15 known-malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin JARs / extracted plugin directories on developer workstations. File path + plugin ID is the highest-fidelity pivot because the plugin IDs are unique campaign artefacts. Rationale: Anchored on the 15 plugin IDs explicitly named in the Aikido report and confirmed by BleepingComputer's independent analysis of ord.cp.code.ai.kit. Plugin IDs are unique campaign artefacts so false positives are essentially nil. Cross-checked with the BleepingComputer article body listing all IDs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate JetBrains plugin updates that happen to share a similar naming convention (very unlikely given the exact IDs)
  • Security researcher / IR team intentionally pulling the samples into a lab
  • Plugin ID collision in a legitimate marketplace package (no such collision observed)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host, the developer account, and which plugin ID dropped. Cross-reference with DeviceProcessEvents for the JetBrains IDE process that wrote the file. 2) Contain: isolate the workstation in Defender; instruct the developer to immediately rotate any OpenAI, DeepSeek, SiliconFlow, and other AI provider API keys saved in IDE settings; uninstall the plugin from the JetBrains Marketplace and disable plugin auto-install for the user group. 3) Hunt: pivot on developer account to find other workstations with the same plugin; query SaaS provider billing/usage logs for the rotated AI keys to detect attacker abuse before rotation.

JetBrains IDE outbound to attacker C2 39.107.60.51 over plaintext HTTP AICommand & Control High
Alerting detection for the campaign's hardcoded C2/exfil endpoint. Matches any outbound network connection from a JetBrains IDE process to 39.107.60.51 — this is where both the stolen API keys leave and the resold keys arrive. Rationale: 39.107.60.51 is the hardcoded C2/exfil endpoint named in the Aikido report and reproduced verbatim in the BleepingComputer article. Process scope to JetBrains IDE binaries (and bundled javaw.exe which executes plugin JARs) makes this near-zero-FP. We also keep the bare ImNetworkSession filter for Sentinel so the IP hit fires regardless of which sensor reported it. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/

  • Customer-support agent reproducing the issue on a developer's machine
  • Sinkholed / takedown traffic if the IP is later seized
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the JetBrains IDE process, plugin directory contents, and the developer account. Pull the AdditionalFields from the network event to confirm the URI path /api/software/key. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-rotate every AI provider API key the developer has stored in JetBrains settings (OpenAI, DeepSeek, SiliconFlow, Anthropic, etc.); add 39.107.60.51 to perimeter blocklist. 3) Hunt: sweep DeviceNetworkEvents and proxy logs across the org for any other host that has contacted 39.107.60.51 — even non-developer machines if the proxy is shared.

Outbound HTTP request to URI path /api/software/key (plugin exfil endpoint) AIActions on Objectives High
URI-based detection for the campaign's exfil path. The path /api/software/key is the literal endpoint the plugins POST stolen AI API keys to. Catches variants of the campaign that may rotate IP/host but keep the URI. Rationale: Path /api/software/key is the literal exfil URI named in the article and quoted in the IOC list — short, vendor-specific, and not a path any legitimate AI provider serves. Catches the campaign even if attackers move off 39.107.60.51 to a new front. Cross-checked with the original Aikido write-up referenced by BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/
ATT&CKT1041 T1567
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal product that happens to expose an unrelated /api/software/key endpoint (rare — exclude known internal hostnames)
  • Security tooling replaying captured PCAPs of the campaign for IR practice
  • License-key servers in pre-existing third-party software (exclude known good hosts)
Suppression filter
| where not (DestinationHostName endswith ".corp.local" or RequestURL startswith "https://internal-licensing.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the request body if proxy logs include it; confirm the IDE process initiated the call. Cross-check the destination IP — current campaign uses 39.107.60.51 but the URI may stay constant across IP rotations. 2) Contain: rotate all AI provider API keys the affected developer has stored in JetBrains; block the destination IP and URI pattern at the perimeter; quarantine the plugin directory. 3) Hunt: search proxy logs for the same URI from any other host in the previous 30 days; check whether the destination uses a different IP in earlier hits (campaign infra rotation).

JetBrains IDE plaintext HTTP to bare-IP destination (no domain) — plugin exfil shape AICommand & Control Medium
Hunting query for the broader campaign-shape: any JetBrains IDE process making plaintext HTTP (port 80) calls directly to a bare IPv4 (no DNS resolution / no Host header domain). Legitimate JetBrains products always talk to *.jetbrains.com / *.openai.com / etc over HTTPS, so this shape is anomalous. Rationale: JetBrains IDEs talk to known cloud endpoints (jetbrains.com, plugins.jetbrains.com, openai.com, anthropic.com, deepseek.com, etc.) over HTTPS. Plaintext HTTP to a bare IPv4 with no host-header domain is the campaign's signature — confirmed by the 39.107.60.51 IP and HTTP scheme in both the Aikido report and the BleepingComputer reproduction. Hunting tier because new dev environments and self-hosted Maven/JFrog mirrors can trip this — see FP filters. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Self-hosted Maven / JFrog Artifactory / npm proxy reached by IP rather than DNS
  • Internal CI/CD container registry on a private network IP exposed via NAT
  • Developer testing a local microservice from inside the IDE's HTTP Client tool
  • Legacy on-prem package mirror that hasn't been migrated to TLS
  • Pre-installed JetBrains license server reached by IP
Suppression filter
| where DstIpAddr !in ("<artifactory-ip>","<jfrog-ip>","<internal-pypi-ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: list distinct destination IPs per developer host; for each unknown IP, WHOIS + passive DNS to determine if it's a corporate asset. Pull plugin directory contents on top hits. 2) Contain: where the IP matches the Aikido IOC list (or any other suspect Chinese-net-block IP), rotate that developer's AI provider keys and isolate the workstation; for unknown destinations, add to monitoring before blocking. 3) Hunt: pivot the destination IP across all sources for 30 days; check JetBrains plugin install events from the host in the same window; look for cluster of developer hosts sharing the same suspicious destination.

Prevent npm and Python Supply Chain Attacks on Developer Machines with Package Configs

StepSecurity
2026-06-16 4 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

npm and Python supply chain attacks run on developer machines and steal secrets. See how Package Configs audits registry, cooldown, and auth across your fleet

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Install of TeamPCP Miasma/Hades-compromised npm or PyPI package versions
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Post-install node or python child process beaconing to non-registry public destination
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Package-manager install descendant reads .npmrc / pip.conf credentials
Install of TeamPCP Miasma/Hades-compromised npm or PyPI package versions AIDelivery High
Hunts file-system evidence of the specific compromised package@version pairs (ensmallen 0.8.101, mflux-streamlit 0.0.3/0.0.4, embiggen 0.11.97, gpsea 0.9.14, pyphetools 0.9.120, nhmpy 2.4.7, ppkt2synergy 0.1.1) being unpacked into node_modules or site-packages on developer endpoints. Article-specific because it pivots on the named IOCs from the June 3/8 2026 campaign, not on a generic package-install template. Rationale: Uses the exact IOC package names from the kill-chain block (Miasma npm wave June 3 / Hades PyPI wave June 8 2026). Anchoring on node_modules/site-packages path plus the named packages avoids false positives from generic file-create noise. Cross-checked StepSecurity blog and MITRE T1195.002. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally fetching IOC samples for analysis
  • Internal mirror legitimately serving an old, clean version of the package name reused after maintainer recovery
  • Air-gapped reproduction lab unpacking previously archived tarballs
  • CI runner reproducing a historical lockfile resolution for incident-response purposes
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("7z.exe","WinRAR.exe","tar.exe") and FolderPath !contains @"\IR-Samples\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the package@version on disk matches an IOC version; pull package.json/PKG-INFO and the resolved-from URL (npm cache / pip wheel cache). 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, revoke all npm and PyPI tokens accessible from that user (~/.npmrc, ~/.pypirc, keyring), force-rotate any cloud SSO refresh tokens, and block the IOC versions at the internal Artifactory/Nexus mirror. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for other endpoints that resolved the same registry hosts in the last 14 days, audit npm/PyPI publish events under that user's tokens for republished tarballs, and verify no downstream repos have lockfiles pinning the bad versions.

Package-manager install descendant reads .npmrc / pip.conf credentials AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects credential-bearing config reads (.npmrc, .yarnrc, .yarnrc.yml, bunfig.toml, .pypirc, pip.conf) by short-lived processes whose ancestor is npm/pnpm/yarn/bun/pip — the exact harvest behaviour Miasma/Hades use to steal publishing tokens. Article-specific because the file set and parent-process set are taken directly from the campaign write-up. Rationale: Article explicitly names the credential files harvested by Miasma/Hades ("a static token sitting in a .npmrc is not just a hygiene issue, it is the fuel these worms run on"). Pairing the named files with package-manager ancestors gives strong intent signal without flagging routine editor opens. Cross-checked StepSecurity write-up and MITRE T1552.001. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running `npm whoami` or `pip config list` which legitimately reads the same config files
  • IDE language-server (VS Code Python/Node extensions) parsing the user's config on workspace open
  • CI bootstrap step that reads .npmrc to set up authenticated proxy
  • Secrets-scanning agent (gitleaks, trufflehog) inventorying dotfiles
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "whoami" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "config list" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "config get"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the originating npm/pip install command line and the package being installed; correlate against advisory feeds for known-compromised versions in the last 24h. 2) Contain: rotate npm/PyPI publishing tokens for the affected user, revoke any GitHub PATs scoped from the same machine, and quarantine the endpoint pending image rebuild. 3) Hunt: check npm/PyPI registry audit logs for publishes from the user's account in the last 7 days, search the fleet for additional installs of the same package@version, and verify cooldown policy is now enforced on the user's package-manager config.
let creds = dynamic([".npmrc",".yarnrc",".yarnrc.yml","bunfig.toml",".pypirc","pip.conf"]);
let pmParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","npm-cli.js","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","bun.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","npm","pip","node","python","python3"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ (creds)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (pmParents) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (pmParents)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType
title: Package Manager Descendant Reads Registry Credentials
id: f5d76a82-3a8d-44e6-b7ef-13c69e2e6451
description: Reads of .npmrc, .yarnrc, bunfig.toml, .pypirc, pip.conf by npm/pnpm/yarn/bun/pip/node/python — the harvest step in Miasma/Hades worm chains.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.credential_access
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_file:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.npmrc'
      - '\.yarnrc'
      - '\.yarnrc.yml'
      - '\bunfig.toml'
      - '\.pypirc'
      - '\pip.conf'
  selection_parent:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\bun.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
  condition: selection_file and selection_parent
level: medium
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) (@TargetFilename:(*\\.npmrc OR *\\.yarnrc OR *\\.yarnrc.yml OR *\\bunfig.toml OR *\\.pypirc OR *\\pip.conf) OR @file.path:(*/.npmrc OR */.yarnrc OR */.yarnrc.yml OR */bunfig.toml OR */.pypirc OR */pip.conf)) (@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\bun.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\pip.exe OR *\\pip3.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/node OR */npm OR */pnpm OR */yarn OR */bun OR */python* OR */pip*))
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| TargetFileName=/(\\\.npmrc|\\\.yarnrc(\.yml)?|\\bunfig\.toml|\\\.pypirc|\\pip\.conf|\/\.npmrc|\/\.yarnrc(\.yml)?|\/bunfig\.toml|\/\.pypirc|\/pip\.conf)$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(node|npm|pnpm|yarn|bun|python3?|pip3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN (".npmrc",".yarnrc",".yarnrc.yml","bunfig.toml",".pypirc","pip.conf")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_path IN ("*\\node.exe","*\\python.exe","*\\python3","*\\pip*","*\\npm*","*\\yarn*","*\\pnpm*","*\\bun*","*/node","*/python*","*/pip*") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN (".npmrc",".yarnrc",".yarnrc.yml","bunfig.toml",".pypirc","pip.conf")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_path IN ("*\\node.exe","*\\python.exe","*\\python3","*\\pip*","*\\npm*","*\\yarn*","*\\pnpm*","*\\bun*","*/node","*/python*","*/pip*") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Post-install node or python child process beaconing to non-registry public destination AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for node/python (descended from an npm or pip install) making outbound network connections to public destinations that are NOT the legitimate package registries — the egress channel a Miasma/Hades post-install script would use to exfil harvested tokens or pull the next stage. Article-specific because it pivots on the install-time parent chain plus the explicit registry destination set named in the article. Rationale: Article identifies the public registries as the legitimate egress endpoints ("registry is their highway") — any node/python descended from an install talking to anything else is the suspicious shape. Sentinel variant restructured to use SrcHostname (per validator suggestion) and an ImProcessCreate prefilter for hosts running the install chain, since ImDnsActivity lacks a process column. Cross-checked StepSecurity write-up and MITRE T1071.001. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package post-install script legitimately fetching binary deps from GitHub Releases or npmjs.com (e.g. esbuild, prebuild-install, node-gyp downloading prebuilt binaries)
  • Telemetry/error reporting from packages like sentry-cli or pytest-sentry
  • Developer running npx of a script that legitimately calls a SaaS API
  • Internal package post-install that reaches the corporate license server (catch by allowing *.internal)
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com","githubusercontent.com","objects.githubusercontent.com") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("prebuild-install","node-gyp","esbuild"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the install command line, package@version, and the post-install script (look in node_modules/<pkg>/package.json `scripts.postinstall` or setup.py); reverse the destination domain via WHOIS / passive DNS. 2) Contain: kill the install process, rotate the user's npm and PyPI tokens, block the destination at the proxy, and snapshot ~/.npmrc and ~/.pypirc before image rebuild. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for any other endpoint that DNS-resolved the same destination in the last 14 days, pivot to npm/PyPI publish events under the user's tokens for republished tarballs, and verify the bad package@version is now blocked at the internal mirror.
let pmAncestors = dynamic(["npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","bun.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","npm","pip"]);
let allowedRegistries = dynamic(["registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com"]);
let installers = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (pmAncestors) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (pmAncestors)
    | where FileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
    | project InstallTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, InstallerPid = ProcessId, InstallerName = FileName, InstallerCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any (allowedRegistries))
| join kind=inner installers on $left.DeviceId == $right.DeviceId, $left.InitiatingProcessId == $right.InstallerPid
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InstallTime, InstallerCmd
| order by Timestamp desc
let allowedRegistries = dynamic(["registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com"]);
let endpointHosts = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","pnpm","yarn","bun","pip","pip3")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","python","python3")
    | summarize by DvcHostname;
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SrcHostname in (endpointHosts)
| where not (DnsQuery has_any (allowedRegistries))
| where DnsQuery !endswith ".internal" and DnsQuery !endswith ".corp" and DnsQuery !endswith ".local"
| where DnsResponseCodeName == "NOERROR" or isempty(DnsResponseCodeName)
| summarize ResolvedHits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Domains = make_set(DnsQuery, 50) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/node OR */python OR */python3)) -@DestinationHostname:(*registry.npmjs.org OR *registry.yarnpkg.com OR *pypi.org OR *files.pythonhosted.org OR *npm.pkg.github.com OR *.internal OR *.corp OR *.local)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ContextImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(node|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName!=/(registry\.npmjs\.org|registry\.yarnpkg\.com|pypi\.org|files\.pythonhosted\.org|npm\.pkg\.github\.com)$/i | ContextImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(node|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i}, field=aid)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app IN ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","python3","node") AND All_Traffic.dest_category="external" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | search NOT (dest IN ("registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com")) | search NOT (dest="*.internal" OR dest="*.corp") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app IN ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","python3","node") AND All_Traffic.dest_category="external" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | search NOT (dest IN ("registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com")) | search NOT (dest="*.internal" OR dest="*.corp") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents

LobeHub /webapi/proxy POST from scripted / non-browser User-Agent AIDelivery High
Detects unauthenticated POST requests to LobeHub's CVE-2026-54157 SSRF endpoint (`/webapi/proxy`) issued by curl/wget/python/PowerShell clients. Legitimate traffic to this route comes from the LobeHub web UI inside a browser; CLI / library user-agents touching it are extremely likely to be exploitation attempts. Rationale: Article shows the working PoC is `curl -X POST ... https://app.lobehub.com/webapi/proxy` — the endpoint is reachable from CLI without any auth, so attacker traffic shape will always be scripted-client UA. The LobeHub web UI invokes this from in-browser JS, so any non-browser UA on this exact path is high-fidelity exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal synthetic monitoring (Datadog Synthetics, Pingdom, Site24x7) probing the proxy endpoint as a health-check
  • CI/CD release-validation scripts using curl/python-requests against staging LobeHub
  • Security team's own SSRF mitigation tests against patched instances
  • Third-party LobeHub SDKs / mobile apps that send a non-browser UA
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "DatadogSynthetics" and RequestClientApplication !has "Pingdom" and RequestClientApplication !has "Site24x7"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full POST body and check whether the URL the attacker proxied targets internal IPs, cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), or returned a reflected Set-Cookie — those upgrade severity instantly. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the edge / WAF and, on the LobeHub side, confirm package version is >2.1.56 with the `checkAuth()` patch applied; if not, hot-patch by adding the auth wrapper or removing the route. 3) Hunt: pivot on `SourceIP` for additional `/webapi/proxy` POSTs, search Clerk auth logs for `__session` values that match any reflected cookie, and review egress from LobeHub server IP for unexpected outbound during the same window.
let suspicious_ua = dynamic(["curl","wget","python-requests","python-urllib","go-http-client","powershell","httpie","libwww","java/","axios","node-fetch","nuclei","ffuf","gobuster"]);

LobeHub /webapi/proxy SSRF body targets internal IP or cloud-metadata endpoint AIReconnaissance High
Detects POST requests to LobeHub's `/webapi/proxy` whose body URL points at RFC1918 internal ranges, loopback, `169.254.169.254` (AWS IMDS), `metadata.google.internal`, `metadata.azure.com`, or `file://`. These are the canonical SSRF targets attackers will pivot to once they discover the unauthenticated proxy. Rationale: Article PoC explicitly demonstrates POST-body URL fetching, and the GHSA confirms the only filter is `ssrfSafeFetch` — which historically has been bypassed via DNS rebinding and IPv6 mapping. Attacker bodies hitting metadata/loopback are the canonical post-discovery move; legitimate URL-preview traffic targets public domains only. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346
ATT&CKT1190 T1526 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised pentest or bug-bounty researcher re-testing the SSRF fix
  • Internal red team exercise scoped to the LobeHub asset
  • Misconfigured client app accidentally sending an internal hostname in the URL preview
  • Security scanner (Nuclei, Burp) running an SSRF template in a maintenance window
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the exact SSRF target URL from the POST body and the HTTP response code/size — non-zero bodies returning AWS metadata JSON (`AccessKeyId`, `SecretAccessKey`) is an active credential-theft incident. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the edge, rotate any IAM role credentials attached to the LobeHub Vercel/EC2 identity, and upgrade LobeHub to >2.1.56 immediately. 3) Hunt: pull all CloudTrail events for the role/instance within the SSRF window for new credential use, search for the same source IP attempting other `/webapi/*` paths, and review for `__session` / `__clerk_db_jwt` cookie reflection (UC3).
let ssrf_patterns = dynamic(["127.0.0.","10.0.0.","192.168.","172.16.","172.17.","172.18.","172.19.","172.20.","172.21.","172.22.","172.23.","172.24.","172.25.","172.26.","172.27.","172.28.","172.29.","172.30.","172.31.","169.254.169.254","metadata.google.internal","metadata.azure.com","localhost","0.0.0.0","file://"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/webapi/proxy"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where Message has_any (ssrf_patterns)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LobeHub /webapi/proxy response reflects Clerk session cookie with Domain=lobehub.com AIExploitation High
Detects the response-side signature of the CVE-2026-54157 cookie-injection chain: `/webapi/proxy` reflects an attacker-controlled `Set-Cookie` whose name matches Clerk's auth cookies (`__session`, `__clerk_db_jwt`, `__client_uat`) and whose `Domain=` is `lobehub.com`. This is the session-fixation primitive against logged-in users. Rationale: Article's second PoC is a direct demonstration: the proxy reflects upstream `Set-Cookie: __session=malicious;Domain=lobehub.com` verbatim — only `Content-Encoding` and `Content-Length` are stripped. Clerk's three documented cookies (`__session`, `__clerk_db_jwt`, `__client_uat`) being set on `lobehub.com` from the proxy route can only happen via this bug. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://clerk.com/docs/security/cookies
ATT&CKT1539 T1606.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • LobeHub's own Clerk auth endpoints legitimately issuing these cookies (different path — `/api/auth/*`, not `/webapi/proxy`)
  • Misconfigured upstream the proxy is fetching that coincidentally sets unrelated cookies named similarly
  • QA / staging environment intentionally injecting test cookies via the proxy
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the reflected cookie value and the source IP that triggered the response — note any victim browser IPs in adjacent `/webapi/proxy` interactions that may have stored the cookie. 2) Contain: invalidate Clerk sessions matching the reflected `__session` / `__clerk_db_jwt` values (Clerk Dashboard → Sessions → Revoke), block the source IP, and force `checkAuth()` patch via emergency LobeHub upgrade. 3) Hunt: pull Clerk audit logs for sign-ins that used the fixed cookie value, review subsequent privileged actions on those accounts, and search webserver logs for repeated proxy POSTs from referrer pages outside `app.lobehub.com` (CSRF stage).
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/webapi/proxy"
| where Message has "Set-Cookie"
| where Message has_any ("__session","__clerk_db_jwt","__client_uat")
| where Message matches regex @"(?i)Domain=\.?lobehub\.com"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Self-hosted LobeHub node process making outbound to internal / metadata IP (post-exploit SSRF) AIActions on Objectives Medium
For organisations running the npm `@lobehub/lobehub` package (≤2.1.56) on their own hosts: detects the LobeHub node.js server process initiating outbound connections to RFC1918 ranges, loopback, or cloud-metadata endpoints — the host-side smoking gun of CVE-2026-54157 being exploited against a self-hosted instance. Rationale: Article flags the npm package `@lobehub/lobehub <=2.1.56` is affected, meaning self-hosted deployments running node.js are in scope. Article also confirms the proxy reaches Vercel's management plane — on customer deployments, the equivalent target is the IMDS / private network. Outbound from the LobeHub node process to RFC1918 or 169.254.169.254 is the host-side fingerprint. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://www.npmjs.com/package/@lobehub/lobehub
ATT&CKT1526 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node.js HTTP client legitimately calling internal microservices (Redis, internal API)
  • cloud-init / SSM Agent / IMDSv2 credential refresh from the same host (different process)
  • Container orchestrator probes from the node sidecar against link-local
  • Self-hosted LobeHub instance with a documented internal proxy/RAG backend at an RFC1918 address
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "healthcheck" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--prometheus"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source host is running `@lobehub/lobehub` (check package.json / running process command line) and that the destination is not a known internal microservice. Pull the upstream WAF/proxy log for matching `/webapi/proxy` POSTs in the same time window. 2) Contain: isolate the LobeHub host, rotate any IAM role / service-account credentials reachable from its metadata endpoint, and upgrade to >2.1.56 before re-attaching to network. 3) Hunt: search cloud audit logs (CloudTrail / Azure Activity / GCP audit) for API calls using credentials originating from the LobeHub instance role within the SSRF window; review egress for the same node PID making subsequent calls.
