Vulnerable LobeHub <=2.1.56 in Defender / Sentinel vulnerability inventory AIWeaponization High
Asset-level detection: surfaces hosts where Defender's vulnerability inventory has identified CVE-2026-54157 (LobeHub `@lobehub/lobehub` ≤2.1.56). Pairs the finding with internet-exposure metadata so SOC can prioritise externally-reachable instances first. Rationale: Article specifies affected versions: `npm:@lobehub/lobehub <=2.1.56`. CveId match plus version-range regex provides a definitive asset hit. Joining DeviceInfo for `IsInternetFacing` lets the SOC prioritise the public-facing instances that the unauthenticated SSRF can be exploited against without any pre-existing access. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://www.npmjs.com/package/@lobehub/lobehub
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.002
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped or lab instance intentionally running an old version for compatibility testing
  • Container image tagged with old version but the running endpoint is already behind a patched reverse proxy that strips `/webapi/proxy`
  • False positive on a derivative/fork that shares the package name but has the auth fix already cherry-picked
  • Vulnerability scanner version-string parsing tripped by a non-semver tag (e.g. `2.1.56-rc1`)
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !endswith "-patched" and SoftwareVersion !endswith "-fixed"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually serves the `/webapi/proxy` route — `curl -X POST https://<host>/webapi/proxy -d 'https://example.com'` returning the example.com body proves exposure; if it returns 401 the auth wrapper is in place. 2) Contain: for internet-facing instances, immediately block POST to `/webapi/proxy` at the WAF/reverse-proxy until upgrade lands; for internal ones, schedule emergency upgrade to >2.1.56. 3) Hunt: for every confirmed-vulnerable host, run UC1–UC3 lookbacks against its access logs for the prior 30 days to detect any exploitation that occurred before patching.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI SSRF: outbound to cloud metadata or RFC1918 from crawler process AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the Crawl4AI Docker server (python/uvicorn/gunicorn process) making outbound HTTP requests to cloud metadata IPs (169.254.169.254), AliCloud (100.100.100.200), or RFC1918/loopback ranges. Covers CWE-918 in /crawl, /md, /llm, /crawl/job webhook and the IPv6-mapped IPv4 bypass (::ffff:169.254.169.254 / ::ffff:10.0.0.1) which the engine normalizes back to IPv4 before connecting. Rationale: Article names exact SSRF targets: 169.254.169.254 cloud metadata, RFC1918, link-local, loopback, and the IPv6-mapped IPv4 bypass (::ffff:169.254.169.254). Crawl4AI uses Python/uvicorn + headless Chromium (playwright) — pinning the initiating process narrows to the Docker container. Cross-checked GitHub advisory and Crawl4AI Docker server source. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.005 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Crawl4AI use against an internal lab/intranet target the team intentionally crawls
  • Container-to-container service mesh calls (envoy/sidecar) on RFC1918
  • Health-check or readiness probe hitting localhost from the crawler
  • Cloud-provider metadata queried by a sidecar agent (CloudWatch agent / IMDS-based SDK) running in the same container/pod
  • Outbound to private DNS resolver in the VPC
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","readiness","liveness") or RemoteUrl has_any ("/healthz","/readyz","/metrics"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full destination URL/host from network logs and correlate to the inbound /crawl, /md, /llm, /screenshot, /pdf, /crawl/job or /llm/job request in the Crawl4AI access log (same client IP within ~5s). Check if RemoteIP == 169.254.169.254 — IMDS theft is critical. 2) Contain: block egress from the Crawl4AI container to RFC1918 / link-local at the host firewall or k8s NetworkPolicy; rotate any IAM role credentials attached to the host (IMDSv2 hop-limit=1 + tokens). Upgrade to patched Crawl4AI. 3) Hunt: search CloudTrail for AssumeRole / GetSessionToken / sts:* from the container's instance-role within 24h of the SSRF; pivot on the requesting source IP for repeat probes; check for internal service responses written back to disk via /screenshot or /pdf output_path.
let MetadataIPs = dynamic(["169.254.169.254","100.100.100.200","fd00:ec2::254"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in (MetadataIPs) or RemoteIPType in ("Private","Loopback","LinkLocal")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn","chrome","chromium","headless_shell")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","crawl4ai.server","deploy.docker.server","playwright")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, RemoteIPType
| order by Timestamp desc
let MetadataIPs = dynamic(["169.254.169.254","100.100.100.200","fd00:ec2::254"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (MetadataIPs)
    or ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr)
    or DstIpAddr startswith "127."
    or DstIpAddr startswith "169.254."
| where NetworkApplicationProtocol in~ ("http","https") or DstPortNumber in (80,443,8080,8443)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI /execute_js endpoint POST — arbitrary JavaScript RCE vector AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP POST requests to the Crawl4AI /execute_js endpoint (default Docker port 11235). On <=0.8.6 this executes arbitrary JS in the server's headless browser with --disable-web-security on, providing JS RCE plus a second SSRF channel. Pre-patch deployments where the operator hasn't set CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED=false will respond 200; the endpoint should rarely be invoked externally. Rationale: Article cites the exact endpoint string '/execute_js' and notes --disable-web-security was on by default; the Docker compose file ships the service on port 11235. Pinning HTTP method=POST + URI=/execute_js + the Crawl4AI listening port gives a high-fidelity exploit indicator since this endpoint is rarely exercised by legitimate clients. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai/blob/main/docker-compose.yml
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal QA / pen test using the endpoint legitimately
  • An authorized Crawl4AI client app that legitimately depends on /execute_js
  • Smoke tests in CI/CD pipelines hitting /execute_js after deploy
  • Authenticated user invoking the endpoint after operator explicitly set CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED=true
Suppression filter
| where not (cIP in ("10.0.0.5","10.0.0.6") or csUserAgent has_any ("GitHub-Actions","crawl4ai-internal"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the request body and source IP from the access log; if the JS body contains fetch() to internal hosts, IMDS, file:// or websocket() it's exploitation, not testing. Confirm the Crawl4AI version (curl /health) — if <=0.8.6 and CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED unset, assume the endpoint is live. 2) Contain: set CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED=false and restart the container; if internet-exposed, restrict ingress to the management API to known CIDRs. Upgrade to patched version. 3) Hunt: review prior week of /execute_js POSTs by source IP, correlate to outbound DNS / connections from the headless browser process (chromium/headless_shell) for SSRF artifacts, and check for /screenshot or /pdf with output_path traversal from the same caller.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (11235, 80, 443, 8000, 8080) or LocalPort in (11235, 80, 443, 8000, 8080)
| where RemoteUrl has "/execute_js" or AdditionalFields has "/execute_js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has "/execute_js"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, sPort, csUserAgent),
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/execute_js"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication),
(ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has "/execute_js"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, HttpMethod, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI unauthenticated /monitor/* access (auth-bypass CWE-306) AIReconnaissance High
Detects HTTP requests to Crawl4AI /monitor/* endpoints (including destructive /monitor/actions/cleanup and the /monitor/ws websocket). On <=0.8.6 the monitor router was mounted without the token_dep dependency, so any unauthenticated request that returns 2xx (rather than 401/403) indicates the vulnerable build. Particularly interesting are calls without an Authorization header or with absent/forged JWT (covers the CWE-798 hardcoded 'mysecret' JWT signing key). Rationale: Advisory names the exact vulnerable routes: /monitor (router-wide), /monitor/actions/cleanup and the /monitor/ws WebSocket. Fix added dependencies=[Depends(token_dep)], so any successful (2xx/3xx) /monitor request on <=0.8.6 means the missing dependency was exploited or scanned. Pair with the CWE-798 default 'mysecret' JWT — attackers can either skip auth entirely or forge a token. Cross-checked GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg and Crawl4AI server router source. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai • https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/306.html • https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1078 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator's local browser hitting the monitor dashboard during normal ops
  • Container/Kubernetes health probes pinging /monitor/ws or a similar status URL
  • Authorized internal IP scanners (Nessus/Qualys) hitting /monitor as part of weekly sweeps
  • Legitimate authenticated admin POSTing to /monitor/actions/cleanup after the operator upgrades and re-introduces auth
  • Mass internet scanners (Shodan/Censys/Project Sonar) probing the endpoint without auth
Suppression filter
| where not (cIP in ("10.0.0.5","10.0.0.6") or csUserAgent has_any ("kube-probe","Prometheus","GoogleHC","ELB-HealthChecker","Datadog Agent"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify Crawl4AI server version (curl /health or container image tag); if <=0.8.6 the monitor is unauthenticated by default. Capture source IP, full URI (especially /monitor/actions/cleanup), and whether the response was 2xx. If success returned the dashboard JSON to a non-allowlisted IP, treat as confirmed exploitation. 2) Contain: front the container with a reverse proxy that enforces Authorization, set a strong CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN and SECRET_KEY (>=32 chars), restrict ingress on management ports (11235), and upgrade. 3) Hunt: search 30d back for /monitor/* 2xx from external IPs; for any matching IP, look for subsequent /execute_js, /screenshot, /pdf (output_path traversal) or /crawl with internal/metadata URLs from the same source.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/monitor" or AdditionalFields has "/monitor"
| where RemotePort in (11235, 80, 443, 8000, 8080)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true

| where csUriStem startswith "/monitor"

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserName, csUserAgent, AuthMissing

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/monitor"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, EventOutcome, RequestClientApplication, Message),
(ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/monitor"
| extend AuthMissing = isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, AuthMissing, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| where HttpStatusCode < 400)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI POST /crawl sandbox-escape payload (gi_frame/f_back/f_builtins chain) AIExploitation High
Hunts for HTTP requests to the Crawl4AI /crawl endpoint whose body contains the CVE-2026-53753 AST sandbox-escape primitives — generator frame attributes (gi_frame, f_back, f_builtins) plus __import__ inside a JsonCssExtractionStrategy schema. These tokens have no benign purpose in a Crawl4AI extraction schema and are the canonical exploit signature. Rationale: gi_frame / f_back / f_builtins are the precise Python frame-object attributes the GHSA names as the sandbox-escape chain (they bypass the underscore-prefix attribute filter in _safe_eval_expression). JsonCssExtractionStrategy is the explicit schema key the attacker abuses. None of these strings appear in legitimate Crawl4AI request bodies — extraction schemas reference CSS selectors and field types, never CPython frame internals. Requires HTTP request-body logging at the proxy/WAF layer; called out in expected_fp_scenarios. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qxjp-w3pj-48m7 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53753
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers / pentesters running PoC scripts (e.g. Burp, sqlmap, custom scanners) against an internal Crawl4AI instance during scheduled testing windows
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nuclei templates, Tenable, Qualys) probing for CVE-2026-53753 — the probe traffic looks identical to live exploitation
  • Internal documentation or unit-test fixtures that legitimately embed the exploit string for regression coverage being scraped or replayed
  • WAF/proxy not configured to ship request bodies — produces silent false negatives, not false positives, but operators may misread the empty result as 'no exploit'
Suppression filter
// Suppress traffic from sanctioned scanner ranges and internal CI testing
| where SourceIP !in ("10.20.30.40","10.20.30.41") // internal Nuclei runners
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nuclei","sqlmap/","NessusFindSubdomains")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull full POST body and source IP from the WAF/proxy log; identify the JsonCssExtractionStrategy computed-field expression that contained gi_frame/f_back. Confirm the destination is a known Crawl4AI deployment and its version (≤ 0.8.6 is vulnerable). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter; if exploitable, isolate the Crawl4AI container (pause/stop, snapshot for forensics) and rotate any secrets the container had access to (cloud IAM, DB creds, JWT signing keys). Patch to fixed Crawl4AI or set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP across all web logs for /crawl recon, then check the container host for shells spawned by python/uvicorn, IMDS access (169.254.169.254), /etc/passwd reads, and outbound connections in the 5 minutes after the request.
// Defender AH does not capture HTTP request bodies; this pivots on outbound from a Crawl4AI container to confirm the parent. Pair with proxy/WAF logs for body inspection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","crawl4ai.deploy","deploy.docker.server")
| where LocalPort in (11235, 8000, 8080)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
// Hunt the exploit string in proxy/WAF/reverse-proxy ingestion (CEF/Syslog → CommonSecurityLog) and W3CIIS if Crawl4AI sits behind IIS.
let SandboxTokens = dynamic(["gi_frame","f_back","f_builtins","__import__","JsonCssExtractionStrategy"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
   | where RequestURL has "/crawl"
   | where Message has_any (SandboxTokens) or DeviceCustomString1 has_any (SandboxTokens) or DeviceCustomString2 has_any (SandboxTokens) or RequestContext has_any (SandboxTokens)
   | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message, DeviceProduct),
  (ImWebSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
   | where Url has "/crawl"
   | where UrlOriginal has_any (SandboxTokens)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, EventProduct))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI/uvicorn parent spawning shells or reconnaissance binaries (post-RCE) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the post-exploitation footprint of CVE-2026-53753: a python/uvicorn/gunicorn process hosting Crawl4AI spawning interactive shells (sh, bash, dash) or recon binaries (curl, wget, nc, whoami, id, uname, hostname). The advisory describes arbitrary OS command execution via os.__import__; the first observable on the host is exactly this parent→child chain. Rationale: The GHSA explicitly states the exploit imports os via __import__ to 'execute arbitrary system commands'. The first OS-level artefact is python/uvicorn spawning a shell or recon utility — Crawl4AI is a headless library that has no legitimate reason to fork /bin/sh, curl, or whoami at runtime. Filter on parent command-line containing 'crawl4ai' / 'deploy.docker.server' to scope to the affected service (those are the canonical entrypoints in the project's Docker server). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qxjp-w3pj-48m7 • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.006 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI container start-up scripts that call /bin/sh to launch supervisord or run entrypoint wrappers (constrain to runtime, not container PID 1 lineage)
  • Operator interactive debugging via docker exec — same parent name, but logon session distinguishable
  • Playwright/Chromium subprocess management spawning /bin/sh -c to set up sandbox profile (filter handled in query but tune per environment)
  • CI/CD pipelines running crawl4ai inside pytest — already filtered, but new test commands may need allowlist
  • Crawler targets that legitimately require curl-equivalent fetching when Crawl4AI is configured to shell out (rare; the library uses Playwright)
Suppression filter
// Already excludes pip install / pytest / setup.py / jupyter / playwright install. Add per-deployment supervisord wrappers as needed:
// | where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("supervisord","entrypoint.sh"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child cmdline and the parent's cwd/container ID. Check if the parent uvicorn process is the Crawl4AI deploy.docker.server (`ps -ef`, `docker ps`); confirm Crawl4AI version is ≤ 0.8.6. Correlate ±5 min with WAF logs for a POST /crawl from an external IP. 2) Contain: stop and snapshot the container (`docker stop`, `docker commit` for forensics), block the source IP, rotate any cloud IAM credentials and JWT secrets accessible from the container, deploy the fixed Crawl4AI image. 3) Hunt: pivot on the container host for IMDS (169.254.169.254) hits, reads of /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /proc/self/environ, ~/.aws/credentials; look for outbound connections to non-target domains from the python process; check for a persisted reverse-shell binary in /tmp or /dev/shm.

Post-RCE credential / environment file access from Crawl4AI container AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access phase that follows successful CVE-2026-53753 RCE: a Crawl4AI-hosted python process or its child reading sensitive secret material — /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /proc/self/environ, ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.docker/config.json, kubernetes service-account tokens. The advisory explicitly calls out attackers being able to 'read/write files and exfiltrate secrets' inside the container. Rationale: The GHSA states the impact is that an attacker 'can execute arbitrary system commands, read/write files, and exfiltrate secrets' from inside the Docker container. /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /proc/self/environ, ~/.aws/credentials and the kubernetes serviceaccount token path are the canonical post-RCE targets in a container environment. Constraining the parent to python/uvicorn with 'crawl4ai' in its cmdline scopes this tightly to the CVE rather than generic container credential-theft. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qxjp-w3pj-48m7
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1083 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI debug/health endpoints that legitimately print environment (e.g. /config/dump prior to the patch — note the fix replaced eval() in /config/dump with Pydantic JSON)
  • Operator running 'docker exec <crawl4ai> printenv' for troubleshooting (interactive session distinguishes)
  • Configuration-management tooling (Ansible, Puppet) reading /etc/passwd inside the container — typically runs under a different parent
  • Custom Crawl4AI extensions that legitimately read AWS credentials via env (uncommon for a scraping workload; verify with app owner)
Suppression filter
// Suppress documented health-check scripts run by container orchestrator if their cmdline is known:
// | where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck.sh","/usr/local/bin/wait-for-it"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child cmdline and parent PID lineage; confirm the parent is the deployed Crawl4AI service and the user is the container's non-root account. Correlate ±5 min with WAF logs for POST /crawl from external. 2) Contain: stop the container and snapshot, rotate every credential reachable from inside (IAM access keys, RDS passwords, JWT secrets, k8s SA token); revoke and re-issue. Patch Crawl4AI to fixed version and set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN. 3) Hunt: search outbound network from the container for the exfil destination (often pastebin, webhook.site, transfer.sh, attacker-controlled HTTPS); search across other Crawl4AI hosts for the same parent→child pattern; pull cloud audit logs (CloudTrail / Azure / GCP) for API calls from the stolen credentials.

Cloud instance metadata (IMDS) access from Crawl4AI container process AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the cloud-credential-theft footprint of CVE-2026-53753 in cloud-hosted Crawl4AI deployments: a python/uvicorn process inside the Crawl4AI container reaching the IMDSv1/v2 endpoint (169.254.169.254, fd00:ec2::254, or metadata.google.internal). Crawl4AI scrapes external web targets and has no legitimate reason to call the cloud metadata service. Rationale: 169.254.169.254 (and the IPv6 fd00:ec2::254 / metadata.google.internal / metadata.azure.com) is the canonical cloud-credential-theft pivot. Crawl4AI is a web-scraping service whose targets are external HTTP(S) endpoints — connections from its python/uvicorn worker to the link-local IMDS IP are intrinsically suspicious. Constraining process name + parent cmdline to crawl4ai distinguishes this from legitimate IMDS callers (kubelet, cloud-init, awscli on the host). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qxjp-w3pj-48m7 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1190 T1078.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Boto3-using Crawl4AI extensions (rare) that legitimately resolve EC2 credentials via IMDS — verify with app owner before suppressing
  • AWS SDK initialization at container start (one-shot at PID 1; differs from runtime python-from-uvicorn pattern)
  • Cloud-init or systemd-networkd reaching IMDS — those run under root/init, not the Crawl4AI service user
  • Kubelet/kube-proxy IMDS access for IRSA — parent will be kubelet, not uvicorn
Suppression filter
// Suppress kubelet IRSA traffic and cloud-init by parent context:
// | where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("kubelet","cloud-init","systemd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the EC2/GCE/Azure VM the container runs on and pull the role/identity attached. From IMDS logs (or VPC Flow), confirm the metadata path requested (e.g. /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role>) and the volume returned. Correlate ±10 min with WAF logs for POST /crawl. 2) Contain: revoke the instance role's credentials immediately (IAM revoke-session, attach a Deny-all policy to the role's session, or detach the role); stop the container; rotate any downstream secrets the role had access to. Patch Crawl4AI. 3) Hunt: search CloudTrail/Azure Activity/GCP audit logs for API calls signed by the role from non-VPC source IPs (sts:GetCallerIdentity from external is the smoking gun); look for the same parent→IMDS pattern across all hosts running Crawl4AI; review any new IAM users/roles or keys created within the past 24h.

// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-53753")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-53753")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Rokarolla dropper distribution site access (infocontablidades.it.com) · [LLM] Sideloaded APK fetch matching Rokarolla Chrome/TikTok masquerade pattern · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Defender / MTD alert pivot for Rokarolla-class Android banker on managed devices
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Rokarolla Android banker C2 beacon to known fallback domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Rokarolla Android banker C2 beacon to known fallback domains AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS resolution or network egress to any of the four Rokarolla C2 fallback domains (beralisvc.info, blestorians.cfd, abiorime.cfd, morevoms.cfd) published by Zimperium. Any hit from a corporate endpoint or BYOD device on the corporate network indicates an active Rokarolla infection. Rationale: All four C2 domains are pulled directly from Zimperium zLabs blog (the original research the Bleeping article cites) — random-looking gibberish strings with zero legitimate corporate use, so any hit is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against Hacker News, Infosecurity Magazine, and hackread reporting of the same campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/rokarolla-android-banker-with-complete-device-takeover-capabilities • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-rokarolla-android-malware-steals.html • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/rokarolla-android-banking-trojan/
ATT&CKT1637 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel researcher sandbox or analyst workstation actively detonating Rokarolla samples on the corporate network
  • Security team using these domains as test indicators in EDR/SIEM validation pipelines
  • Passive DNS / DNS resolver service that pre-resolves indicator lists
  • Newsletter / blog page on the corporate proxy that embeds the IOC strings as text and triggers URL-parsing detection
  • An employee BYOD Android device legitimately quarantined by MTD but still attempting beacons until cleaned
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or RemoteUrl has_any ("beralisvc.info","blestorians.cfd","abiorime.cfd","morevoms.cfd")
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic(["sandbox-malware-01","redteam-detonation-01"]))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the source endpoint/device and the user. If it is an Android phone enrolled in MDE for Mobile / MDM, pull the device's recent app install history and active accessibility-service grants. If it is a Windows/Mac workstation, treat as either a researcher detonation or a tethered Android device — verify with the user. 2) CONTAIN: block all four C2 domains at the corporate DNS/proxy/firewall. If an Android endpoint is implicated, mark the device non-compliant in Intune, push a remote selective wipe, and force-reset the user's banking, crypto wallet, M365, and any accounts whose 2FA SMS could have hit the device. 3) HUNT: pivot on the source IP for any other resolved Rokarolla-class domains (NRD .cfd TLD spike, low-reputation .info), look for prior connections to the distribution host infocontablidades.it.com, and enumerate other Android devices in the fleet that hit the same domains in the last 30 days.
let RokarollaC2 = dynamic(["beralisvc.info","blestorians.cfd","abiorime.cfd","morevoms.cfd"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteUrl has_any (RokarollaC2)
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
 | where RemoteUrl has_any (RokarollaC2)
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType, RemoteUrl, AdditionalFields)
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, DeviceCategory, DeviceType) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| order by Timestamp desc
let RokarollaC2 = dynamic(["beralisvc.info","blestorians.cfd","abiorime.cfd","morevoms.cfd"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(ImDnsActivity
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DnsQuery has_any (RokarollaC2)
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseCodeName, EventProduct),
(DnsEvents
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Name has_any (RokarollaC2)

(CommonSecurityLog

Rokarolla dropper distribution site access (infocontablidades.it.com) AIDelivery High
Detects any DNS, web-proxy, or EDR network event to infocontablidades.it.com — the malicious site Zimperium identified as serving the Rokarolla dropper masquerading as Google Chrome or TikTok. Catches users who visited the lure page from a corporate workstation or whose mobile device used the corporate network during APK fetch. Rationale: infocontablidades.it.com is the exact distribution URL named in the Zimperium blog (hxxps[://]infocontablidades[.]it[.]com/) that serves the fake Chrome/TikTok APK. Highly fidelity — there is no legitimate business reason for a corporate endpoint to reach this lookalike-Italian shell domain. Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/rokarolla-android-banker-with-complete-device-takeover-capabilities • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-rokarolla-android-malware-targets-217-banking-crypto-apps/
ATT&CKT1660 T1608.001
Data sourcesWeb Network_Resolution
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR/malware research detonation referencing the IOC explicitly
  • Security awareness training portal that embeds the live URL as a 'do not click' example and triggers click-tracker prefetch
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment service that probes IOCs from a corporate egress IP
  • Email security gateway that follows URLs in scanned messages and inherits the corporate source IP
  • SOAR playbook with a domain-reputation enrichment step that issues a live HTTP probe
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<sandbox_egress_ip>","<ti_enrichment_egress_ip>"]))
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("VirusTotal","urlscan","PhishTank","ANY.RUN")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the source user/device and pull the full URL chain — was it a click from email, Teams, SMS bridged via Phone Link, or direct navigation? Check the user's mailbox + Teams for the inbound lure message and find every other recipient who got the same link. 2) CONTAIN: sinkhole infocontablidades.it.com at corporate DNS, block at the SWG, and add a Conditional Access block for the user's Android device until MTD/MDM scan completes. If an APK was actually downloaded, isolate the device and reset banking/crypto/M365 credentials whose 2FA SMS could have been intercepted. 3) HUNT: pivot for the four Rokarolla C2 domains (see related UC) on the same source IP, hunt EmailEvents/UrlClickEvents for the same lure URL across all users, and check for Android devices in Intune that installed an APK matching Chrome/TikTok in the last 14 days from a non-Play-Store source.

 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName)
| order by Timestamp desc

(ImWebSession

 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

Defender / MTD alert pivot for Rokarolla-class Android banker on managed devices AIInstallation Medium
Surfaces Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Mobile (and any other MTD partner forwarding to SecurityAlert) alerts on Android devices that map to the Rokarolla technique set: input capture (T1417), input injection (T1516), masquerading as Chrome/Play Protect (T1655.001), or SMS abuse (T1582). Joins to DeviceInfo to confirm OSPlatform=Android and to enrich with the affected user. Rationale: Pivots on Zimperium-published Mobile ATT&CK technique IDs (T1417, T1516, T1655.001, T1582, T1414, T1513, T1660 — all in the Zimperium IOC list) joined to DeviceInfo OSPlatform=Android to suppress non-mobile noise. Skipped Sigma/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch because mobile-MTD alerts don't ship cleanly to those backends. Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/rokarolla-android-banker-with-complete-device-takeover-capabilities
ATT&CKT1655.001 T1417.001 T1516 T1582
Data sourcesAlerts
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MTD telemetry catching legitimate accessibility-using apps (TalkBack, Voice Access, password managers like 1Password/Bitwarden) that hold the same Accessibility permission
  • Mobile penetration testing tools deliberately installed by red team
  • Mobile QA test harness apps that automate UI input across many activities
  • Approved mobile RMM/MDM agents that read SMS for OTP routing (e.g. enterprise SSO push fallback)
  • Banking app's own anti-fraud SDK that fingerprints accessibility usage and triggers MTD heuristics
Suppression filter
| where EntityFile !in~ (dynamic(["com.google.android.marvin.talkback","com.google.android.apps.accessibility.voiceaccess","com.lastpass.lpandroid","com.agilebits.onepassword","com.x8bit.bitwarden"]))
| where AlertName !has_any ("test","demo","simulation")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: open the alert in M365 Defender / Sentinel, identify the user, the Android device (Model + Intune compliance state), and the offending package. Pull the device's accessibility-service-grant history and any recent sideloaded APK installs. Check whether the user's M365 sign-ins from that device show MFA fatigue or SMS-based prompts in the last 7 days. 2) CONTAIN: mark the device non-compliant in Intune → triggers CA block, push selective wipe of corporate data, force a password + MFA-method reset for the user (assume SMS OTP intercepted), revoke M365 refresh tokens, and disable any registered SMS-OTP recovery methods on the user's banking / crypto / personal email accounts. 3) HUNT: query the Rokarolla C2 domains (related UC) and the distribution URL (related UC) against the same user's source IPs from the last 30 days; identify any other Android devices in the tenant with the same package SHA256 or that hit the same C2; review the user's mailbox + Teams for the original lure

Sideloaded APK fetch matching Rokarolla Chrome/TikTok masquerade pattern AIDelivery Medium
Hunts corporate web/proxy traffic and EDR network telemetry for Android APK downloads (Content-Type / file extension .apk) whose filename or referrer impersonates Chrome or TikTok but whose origin host is NOT a Google-controlled domain (play.google.com, googleapis.com, gstatic.com) or TikTok's CDN. Catches Rokarolla droppers regardless of which lure domain rotates in next. Rationale: Pattern is directly derived from the Zimperium description of the dropper masquerading as Chrome and TikTok, plus the article's note that the install screen impersonates Google Play Protect. The Google/TikTok CDN allowlist suppresses the obvious legitimate-distribution false positives while keeping the rare-domain residue that is exactly the Rokarolla shape. Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/rokarolla-android-banker-with-complete-device-takeover-capabilities • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-rokarolla-android-malware-targets-217-banking-crypto-apps/
ATT&CKT1660 T1655.001 T1407
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal MDM/app-distribution server hosting a legitimate repackaged Chrome enterprise APK (e.g. an internal Chromium build for kiosk devices)
  • Mobile QA team sideloading TikTok beta builds from a CI artifact server
  • Android emulator package mirrors (apkpure.com, apkmirror.com) used by developers for legitimate testing
  • Mobile threat-intel team downloading sample APKs to a malware-analysis VM
  • Marketing landing-page generator that auto-includes the text 'Chrome' in download URLs as SEO bait
Suppression filter
| where HttpHostName !in~ (dynamic(["<internal_mdm_host>","<ci_artifact_host>","apkmirror.com","apkpure.com"]))
| where SrcHostname !startswith "sandbox-" and SrcHostname !startswith "redteam-"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: verify whether the source is a known internal MDM/CI host or a sanctioned APK mirror; if so, allowlist it and document. Otherwise, identify the user and check whether the same source IP also resolved the Rokarolla C2 domains or infocontablidades.it.com in the last 14 days. 2) CONTAIN: if the download went to a managed Android device, mark it non-compliant in Intune, push a selective wipe, and walk the user through removing the masquerading package. If the destination Android device is BYOD/unmanaged, contact the user, instruct them to delete the package, and reset all credentials cached on the device (start with banking, crypto, M365, SMS-OTP secondaries). 3) HUNT: pivot the SHA256 of the downloaded APK into VirusTotal / Zimperium / public sandboxes; if it scores as Rokarolla, mass-search the corporate fleet for the same hash, the same originating URL, and any of the four Rokarolla C2 fallback domains over a 90-day window.
let GoogleHosts = dynamic(["play.google.com","googleapis.com","gstatic.com","google.com","googleusercontent.com"]);
let TikTokHosts = dynamic(["tiktokcdn.com","tiktokv.com","byteoversea.com","tiktok.com","musical.ly"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
 | where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)\.apk(\?|$)"
 | where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)(chrome|tiktok|play[_-]?protect)"
 | where not(RemoteUrl has_any (GoogleHosts) or RemoteUrl has_any (TikTokHosts))
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
(DeviceFileEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
 | where FileName endswith ".apk"
 | where FileName matches regex @"(?i)(chrome|tiktok|play[_-]?protect)"
 | where isnotempty(FileOriginUrl) and not(FileOriginUrl has_any (GoogleHosts) or FileOriginUrl has_any (TikTokHosts))
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileSize, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName)
| order by Timestamp desc
let GoogleHosts = dynamic(["play.google.com","googleapis.com","gstatic.com","google.com","googleusercontent.com"]);
let TikTokHosts = dynamic(["tiktokcdn.com","tiktokv.com","byteoversea.com","tiktok.com","musical.ly"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)\.apk(\?|$)" or FileMimeType =~ "application/vnd.android.package-archive"
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)(chrome|tiktok|play[_-]?protect)" or FileName matches regex @"(?i)(chrome|tiktok|play[_-]?protect)"
| where not(HttpHostName has_any (GoogleHosts) or HttpHostName has_any (TikTokHosts))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, FileName, FileMimeType, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpResponseBodyBytes, EventVendor
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 6c8d9e2f-4b5c-4a6d-b1e2-3f5a6b7c8d83
status: experimental
description: Detects HTTP downloads of an Android APK whose URL path impersonates Chrome, TikTok or Google Play Protect but whose host is not a Google or TikTok-owned domain. Pattern matches the Rokarolla Android banking trojan dropper described by Zimperium zLabs.
references:
  - https://zimperium.com/blog/rokarolla-android-banker-with-complete-device-takeover-capabilities
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-rokarolla-android-malware-targets-217-banking-crypto-apps/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1660
  - attack.t1655.001
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  selection_url:
    cs-uri-stem|endswith: '.apk'
  selection_lure:
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - 'chrome'
      - 'tiktok'
      - 'PlayProtect'
      - 'play_protect'
      - 'play-protect'
  filter_google:
    cs-host|endswith:
      - '.google.com'
      - '.googleapis.com'
      - '.gstatic.com'
      - '.googleusercontent.com'
  filter_tiktok:
    cs-host|endswith:
      - '.tiktokcdn.com'
      - '.tiktokv.com'
      - '.byteoversea.com'
      - '.tiktok.com'
  condition: selection_url and selection_lure and not (filter_google or filter_tiktok)
level: medium

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin ID present in IDE plugins folder · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JetBrains IDE process connects to malicious plugin C2 39.107.60.51 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Inspected HTTP POST to /api/software/ with attacker's static X-Api-Key header · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
JetBrains IDE process connects to malicious plugin C2 39.107.60.51 AICommand & Control Medium
JetBrains IDEs run plugins inside the IDE's JVM, so a direct outbound connection from idea64.exe / pycharm64.exe / java.exe to the hardcoded attacker IP 39.107.60.51 is a high-fidelity indicator that one of the 15 malicious AI-assistant plugins has just exfiltrated a stored AI provider API key. The IP is single-purpose and sits in Alibaba Cloud (AS37963) with no legitimate use case for a developer endpoint. Rationale: 39.107.60.51 is the hardcoded plaintext-HTTP exfil server named verbatim in the Aikido write-up (Block 3 / IoC list). A single hit from a developer endpoint is sufficient — no other legitimate caller has been observed for this address.
ATT&CKT1041 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel researcher manually probing the C2 from a sandboxed dev VM
  • Outbound proxy / firewall liveness check explicitly configured to ping the published IOC
  • Sinkhole / decoy traffic from a deliberate honeypot deployment
  • Defender / EDR re-detonation of an archived malicious plugin during retro-hunt
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory / file-event history for the affected host and list every plugin under %APPDATA%\JetBrains\<IDE>\plugins — flag any whose XML plugin id matches the 15 IoCs (org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.json.simple.kit, etc.). Capture the InitiatingProcessAccountUpn — that user typed at least one AI provider API key into the plugin settings. 2) Contain: immediately revoke and rotate any OpenAI / DeepSeek / SiliconFlow API keys belonging to the user; uninstall the offending plugin and remove its directory; block 39.107.60.51 at the egress proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot on plugin id across all developer endpoints (DeviceFileEvents FolderPath has 'JetBrains' and 'plugins'); check OpenAI / DeepSeek billing portals for unusual usage in the last 60 days from unfamiliar IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "39.107.60.51"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, Url, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outbound Connection to JetBrains Marketplace Plugin AI-Key Stealer C2
id: 7c5e1c34-9a4b-4f2e-9b1a-2d6c0e7b1c01
description: Detects outbound network connection to 39.107.60.51, the hardcoded C2 used by 15 malicious JetBrains plugins (Aikido 2026-06-16) to exfiltrate user-supplied OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API keys.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/multiple-jetbrains-ide-plugins-caught-stealing-ai-keys
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1041
  - attack.t1567
  - attack.exfiltration
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    DestinationIp: '39.107.60.51'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:39.107.60.51
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=39.107.60.51
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="39.107.60.51" by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.app, All_Traffic.transport | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="39.107.60.51" by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.app, All_Traffic.transport | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Inspected HTTP POST to /api/software/ with attacker's static X-Api-Key header AIActions on Objectives Medium
Where a TLS-inspecting proxy or web gateway records full request URLs and headers, this catches the actual exfil call — POST http://39.107.60.51/api/software/<name> carrying the hardcoded static token X-Api-Key: F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D and a JSON body containing the victim's apiKey field. This is the most precise rule possible against the campaign because both the URL path and the token are unique to the malicious plugin codebase. Rationale: Both the URI path /api/software/ AND the destination 39.107.60.51 are taken verbatim from the deobfuscated save() handler in the article (Block 2). Either signal alone is unique to this campaign; together they leave no plausible false positive.
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentester replaying the published IOC against a sanctioned target
  • Threat-intel platform retrospectively decoding archived sandbox PCAPs
  • Vendor security scanner generating synthetic exfil traffic for control validation
  • Honeypot infrastructure deliberately calling the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract SourceIP / InitiatingProcessAccountUpn from the POST — that user's stored AI keys are already at the attacker. Identify which JetBrains IDE process (idea64.exe / pycharm64.exe / java.exe) made the call so the responsible plugin id can be tied back via plugin XML. 2) Contain: revoke and rotate every AI provider key (OpenAI / DeepSeek / SiliconFlow) associated with that developer; uninstall the offending plugin directory and clear the plugin's settings file; block 39.107.60.51 and any URI containing /api/software/ at the egress proxy. 3) Hunt: search 90 days of proxy logs for any prior POST to the same URI; pivot on the static header value 'F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D' in raw proxy capture if header logging is enabled; query AI provider billing dashboards for spend anomalies on the victim's keys.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51" or RemoteUrl has "/api/software/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "39.107.60.51" or RequestURL has "/api/software/"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin ID present in IDE plugins folder AIInstallation High
All 15 IoC plugin XML ids (org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.json.simple.kit, com.my.code.tools, ord.cp.code.ai.kit, etc.) are distinctive enough that any file write under %APPDATA%\JetBrains\<IDE>\plugins or ~/.config/JetBrains/<IDE>/plugins that contains one of these identifiers is conclusive evidence the host installed a backdoored plugin from the campaign. This catches the install moment regardless of whether the user has yet pasted an AI API key. Rationale: Plugin XML ids are the canonical, unique identifier JetBrains uses to dedupe Marketplace entries; the 15 ids in the article's IoC table are the verbatim package identifiers and will be present on disk in any installed copy (Marketplace install writes them into the plugin's META-INF). High-fidelity with effectively zero collision risk.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1505.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint forensics tool re-reading a quarantined plugin artifact
  • Backup software touching the JetBrains plugins directory and re-emitting filenames
  • Developer manually examining a benign plugin coincidentally named identically (improbable — these ids are squatted attacker-chosen strings)
  • Security inventory scanner enumerating installed plugin metadata
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate every plugin under %APPDATA%\JetBrains (Win) or ~/Library/Application Support/JetBrains (mac) or ~/.config/JetBrains (Linux) on the host; cross-reference plugin.xml id against the 15 IoCs; pull DeviceNetworkEvents for that host to confirm whether 39.107.60.51 was already contacted (key already exfil'd). 2) Contain: uninstall the plugin via JetBrains Plugins UI (Disable → Restart → Remove), then delete the residual directory; rotate any AI provider API keys that user has used in the IDE in the last 90 days; push EDR-level block for the plugin id strings. 3) Hunt: sweep the entire developer fleet with the same query over 60d to find every infected host; cross-reference vendor accounts (CodePilot/mycode, StackSmith/misshewei, CodeCrafter/keteme, CodeWeaver/simpledev, JetCode/skyblue, DailyCode/dialycode, ZenCoder/947cb4c8-5db1-4cf0-8182-0aae7c433bb3) for any future plugin uploads.
let MaliciousPluginIds = dynamic(["org.sm.yms.toolkit","com.json.simple.kit","org.bug.find.tools","org.translate.ai.simple","com.yy.test.ai.simple","com.dev.ai.toolkit","com.json.view.simple","com.my.git.ai.kit","org.check.ai.ds","com.review.tool.code","org.code.assist.dev.tool","com.coder.ai.dpt","com.my.code.tools","ord.cp.code.ai.kit","com.dp.git.ai.tool"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where FolderPath has "JetBrains" and FolderPath has "plugins"
| where FileName has_any (MaliciousPluginIds) or FolderPath has_any (MaliciousPluginIds)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let MaliciousPluginIds = dynamic(["org.sm.yms.toolkit","com.json.simple.kit","org.bug.find.tools","org.translate.ai.simple","com.yy.test.ai.simple","com.dev.ai.toolkit","com.json.view.simple","com.my.git.ai.kit","org.check.ai.ds","com.review.tool.code","org.code.assist.dev.tool","com.coder.ai.dpt","com.my.code.tools","ord.cp.code.ai.kit","com.dp.git.ai.tool"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where TargetFilePath has "JetBrains" and TargetFilePath has "plugins"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (MaliciousPluginIds) or TargetFileName has_any (MaliciousPluginIds)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
