Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("39.107.60.51") or RemoteUrl has_any ("")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["39.107.60.51"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic([""]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Google Vertex AI SDK Flaw Let Attackers Hijack Model Uploads via Bucket Squatting

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 11 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A flaw in the Google Cloud Vertex AI SDK for Python let an attacker with no access to a victim's project hijack the victim's machine learning model upload and run code inside Google's serving infrastructure. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, which found and reported the bug through Google's bug bounty program, calls the technique "Pickle in the Middle" and said it saw no exploitation in the wild.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Vertex AI Model.upload artifactUri / staging_bucket references cross-project GCS bucket · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Rapid object overwrite race in Vertex AI staging bucket (Pickle-in-the-Middle replacement) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process

GCS bucket creation matching Vertex AI predictable staging pattern (bucket squatting precursor) AIWeaponization Medium
Detects creation of Cloud Storage buckets whose names match the vulnerable SDK's predictable default pattern '<projectId>-vertex-staging-<region>'. Pre-v1.148.0 Vertex AI SDK Model.upload() resolved this exact name with no ownership verification, so an attacker pre-creating it in their own GCP project hijacks the victim's model upload (Unit 42 'Pickle in the Middle'). Rationale: Article names the literal default bucket pattern 'project-vertex-staging-region' and notes v1.144.0 added a uuid4 — so any post-v1.144.0 legit bucket carries a UUID and any name WITHOUT one is either an old vulnerable upload or an attacker's squat. Corroborated by Unit 42's own write-up (unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/) confirming the predictable scheme. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/ • https://focalsecurity.io/blog/kicking-the-bucket-gcp-cross-tenant/
ATT&CKT1583.001 T1583.006
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Vertex AI team manually creating staging bucket that happens to follow the SDK naming convention
  • Internal DR runbook re-creating staging buckets in a new region after project migration
  • Security researcher / red team intentionally exercising the SDK in a sanctioned project
  • Old Vertex AI projects that legitimately seeded the bucket pre-March-2026 and never rotated to uuid4 names
Suppression filter
and not (protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail like /@(yourorg\.com|yourorg-internal\.iam\.gserviceaccount\.com)$/i)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the principalEmail and callerIp of the create call; confirm whether the bucket sits inside the same GCP organisation as the project ID embedded in the bucket name. Out-of-org or unknown IP = high suspicion. 2) Contain: if the create is from an unknown org, escalate to Google Cloud abuse and request takedown; for in-org but unsanctioned buckets, restrict via Organization Policy 'restrict bucket name lexical patterns' or set an iam.allowedPolicyMembers constraint blocking that bucket from receiving aiplatform writes. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same principal across the last 30d for additional '*-vertex-staging-*' or '*-vertex-pipelines-*' creates, and grep Vertex AI Model.upload audit logs for any artifactUri pointing into the squatted bucket — that confirms a successful hijack.
title: GCS Bucket Creation Matching Vertex AI Predictable Staging Name (Bucket Squatting)
id: 9a0c8e21-7b2d-4f31-9c4a-3b8e0f7a1d22
status: experimental
description: Detects creation of a Google Cloud Storage bucket whose name matches the pre-v1.148.0 Vertex AI Python SDK's predictable default staging-bucket pattern '<projectId>-vertex-staging-<region>'. Pre-positioned squatted buckets enable the Unit 42 'Pickle in the Middle' cross-tenant RCE attack.
references:
    - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-vertex-ai-sdk-flaw-let-attackers.html
    - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
    - attack.resource_development
    - attack.t1583.001
    - attack.t1583.006
logsource:
    product: gcp
    service: gcp.audit
detection:
    selection:
        protoPayload.methodName: 'storage.buckets.create'
    bucket_pattern:
        protoPayload.resourceName|re: '.+-vertex-staging-[a-z]+[a-z0-9-]*$'
    filter_uuid_post_patch:
        protoPayload.resourceName|re: '.+-vertex-staging-[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}'
    condition: selection and bucket_pattern and not filter_uuid_post_patch
falsepositives:
    - Internal teams manually creating staging buckets that follow Vertex AI naming convention
    - Migration / DR re-creation of legitimately-owned buckets in a new region
level: medium
source:gcp.audit @protoPayload.methodName:storage.buckets.create (@protoPayload.resourceName:*-vertex-staging-* OR @protoPayload.request.bucket.name:*-vertex-staging-*) -@protoPayload.resourceName:*-vertex-staging-????????-????-????-????-*

Vulnerable google-cloud-aiplatform SDK install detected (<1.148.0) AIWeaponization High
Detects pip / poetry / conda installing google-cloud-aiplatform at a version prior to 1.148.0 — the release that added bucket ownership verification in Model.upload(). Versions 1.139.0-1.143.x are fully vulnerable; 1.144.0-1.147.x are partially patched (random uuid4 only). Flags CI/CD pipelines, notebooks, and dev workstations that are still exposed. Rationale: Article explicitly names the patched versions (1.144.0 partial, 1.148.0 full) and the vulnerable tested versions (1.139.0, 1.140.0). The regex catches the entire vulnerable + partially-patched band 1.139.x–1.147.x. Highest-fidelity defender-side signal because the vulnerability lives client-side in the SDK. Corroborated against Unit 42 timeline. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI pipeline rebuilding from frozen requirements.txt that pins an old version for reproducibility
  • Sandboxed regression tests exercising backward compatibility of the SDK
  • Security team installing the vulnerable version in an isolated lab to reproduce the bug
  • Data scientist running a Jupyter notebook from before April 2026 without a pin update
  • Docker base image scan triggering pip show inside a build container
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("vsls-agent.exe","code.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","--report")) and not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "runner-worker.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "sandbox-regression")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify whether the host is a CI runner, developer workstation, or production prediction container. Pull the InitiatingProcess parent — `code.exe`/`jupyter` is benign developer activity; `dockerd`/`buildkit`/`runner-worker` flags a production-bound artifact and needs immediate escalation. 2) Contain: for any production-bound install, pause the deploy pipeline and force `pip install --upgrade 'google-cloud-aiplatform>=1.148.0'`; do NOT just patch the running image — re-build from a base that pins the safe minimum, since the bug bites at upload time not deploy time. 3) Hunt: pivot on the user to any prior `aiplatform.Model.upload()` or `aiplatform.init()` calls in GCP audit logs for the same project ID; cross-check whether the staging_bucket parameter was set explicitly (safe) or left default (exposed) — search Python source via `grep -r 'staging_bucket=' --include=*.py`.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","poetry.exe","conda.exe","uv.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "google-cloud-aiplatform"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","add","sync","update")
| extend PinnedVersion = extract(@"(?i)google-cloud-aiplatform==(1\.(?:13[0-9]|14[0-7])(?:\.[0-9]+)?)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(PinnedVersion) or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)google-cloud-aiplatform(?!==)"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, PinnedVersion, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip","python","poetry","conda","uv")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "google-cloud-aiplatform"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","add","sync","update")
| extend PinnedVersion = extract(@"(?i)google-cloud-aiplatform==(1\.(?:13[0-9]|14[0-7])(?:\.[0-9]+)?)", 1, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(PinnedVersion) or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)google-cloud-aiplatform(?!==)"
| where ActorUsername !has "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, PinnedVersion, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vertex AI Model.upload artifactUri / staging_bucket references cross-project GCS bucket AIDelivery High
Detects Vertex AI ModelService.UploadModel (or training jobs) whose artifactUri / stagingBucket parameter points to a gs:// bucket that does NOT live in the calling project — the defining signature of the Pickle-in-the-Middle hijack, since the victim SDK silently uploads to the attacker's squatted bucket in a different GCP project. Rationale: Article: 'The victim's SDK would then upload the model files to the attacker's bucket' — the in-the-clear signature is an UploadModel call where artifactUri's bucket project ID != calling project ID. Datadog query surfaces the raw call set; the cross-project comparison is performed at rule-level via groupBy because Datadog log search cannot self-join on two attributes. Splunk's eval-and-compare does the full check inline. Sentinel left empty — GCP audit logs are not in the canonical Sentinel schema list provided. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1554

If the owning project is OUTSIDE your organisation's resource hierarchy, treat as confirmed hijack and proceed to step 2. 2) Contain: revoke the Vertex AI service account's storage.objects.create grant on the foreign bucket via IAM Conditions, then call `aiplatform.Model.delete()` on the just-uploaded model BEFORE Vertex AI reads it (race is ~2.5s — automation only); pause all training pipelines in the affected project until staging_bucket is explicitly pinned. 3) Hunt: enumerate every `aiplatform.init()` and `aiplatform.Model.upload()` in the last 90d in this project, and audit pipeline source for un-pinned staging_bucket; cross-tenant token theft means you must rotate any service-agent credential the deployed model could reach (BigQuery, GKE node SAs).

Rapid object overwrite race in Vertex AI staging bucket (Pickle-in-the-Middle replacement) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the 'Pickle in the Middle' race condition: two storage.objects.create / write events for the same model artifact path (.pkl / .joblib / model.json) within 5 seconds, where the second write is from a different principal than the first. Unit 42 measured 2.5s between upload and Vertex AI read; the PoC overwrote in 1.4s. Rationale: Article: 'Unit 42 measured about 2.5 seconds between the victim's upload and Vertex AI reading the file. In its proof of concept, the attacker used a Cloud Function that triggered after upload and replaced the model in 1.4 seconds.' Detection captures two writes to the same staging-bucket model artifact within a 5s window by distinct principals — the literal signature of the replacement race. Datadog query surfaces the raw write set; the rapid-double-write correlation runs at rule level (Datadog Cloud SIEM groupBy on resourceName with `count >= 2` in 5s and dcount(principalEmail) >= 2). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1565.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vertex AI itself rewriting the staging artifact during training-job preprocessing (single principal — same SA — filters out)
  • Pipeline retry logic re-uploading the same model file after a transient failure
  • DataOps validation step that rewrites model.pkl after lint/signing
  • Versioned model registry workflow that produces multiple artifacts per training run
  • Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle rule overwriting with a tagged copy
Suppression filter
and not (@protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail:service-*@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com AND @protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail_second:service-*@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the two principalEmails on the racing writes — if both are in the same project's service-agent identity (`service-<projectnum>@gcp-sa-aiplatform.iam.gserviceaccount.com` family), it's almost certainly a benign retry; if the second writer is a non-AI service account, especially from a different project number, treat as confirmed exploit. 2) Contain: immediately set the bucket to versioned + WORM (Bucket Lock) to freeze tampering; revoke the foreign principal's storage.objects.create via Deny Policy; mark the just-uploaded model as compromised in your model registry and block Model.deploy() on it. 3) Hunt: pull the artifactUri of the racing model into VirusTotal / static-analyse the pickle stream (`pickletools.dis()`) to confirm executable opcode; pivot the foreign principal across CloudAuditLogs for any IAM read, BigQuery read, or GKE container image listing — those are the post-exploit access patterns the article enumerates.

Vertex AI model deployed with artifactUri pointing to externally-owned GCS bucket AIInstallation High
Detects Vertex AI Model.deploy / DeployedModel registry entries whose underlying model artifactUri resolves to a Cloud Storage bucket not owned by the calling project's organisation. Catches post-hijack persistence — the squatted model survives the race condition only if it's then served, so a deploy referencing a foreign bucket is the smoking gun. Rationale: Article: 'When Vertex AI later loaded the swapped model, the attacker's code executed inside the serving container.' Deployment of a model whose artifactUri retains the pre-uuid4 vulnerable pattern (no UUID component) and lives in a foreign bucket is the persistence-of-hijack signature. Cross-checked against Unit 42's article — they explicitly enumerate the post-exploit damage (BigQuery, GKE, container images, internal tenant logs) reachable from the stolen token, which underscores why catching this at deploy-time matters. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/
ATT&CKT1525 T1036.005 T1199
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Multi-project ML platform legitimately promoting models from a central artifact registry project
  • Use of public Vertex AI Model Garden references that resolve to gs:// URIs in google-owned public buckets
  • Disaster-recovery restore deploying from a previously-archived bucket that retained the old naming
  • Federated research project where partner organisation legitimately owns the staging bucket
  • Legacy Vertex AI projects whose default bucket was created pre-v1.144.0 and never re-issued
Suppression filter
and not (@protoPayload.response.artifactUri:(gs://your-org-modelregistry-* OR gs://your-org-mlplatform-shared-*) OR @protoPayload.response.artifactUri:gs://cloud-samples-data/*)
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve `dest_bucket` to its owning project via `gcloud storage buckets describe gs://<bucket> --format='value(projectNumber)'` and check organisation membership via Cloud Asset Inventory. Foreign org → confirmed compromise. 2) Contain: immediately UndeployModel on the affected Endpoint, then revoke the Vertex AI service agent's token via `gcloud iam service-accounts keys revoke` and force `gcloud auth application-default revoke` on any host that may have cached it; treat the serving container's BigQuery, GKE node SA, and KMS keys as compromised and rotate. 3) Hunt: search BigQuery jobs, GKE container.images.list, and KMS Decrypt audit logs for any call within 24h whose `principalEmail` matches the Vertex AI service agent and `callerIp` is outside Google's published service-agent ranges — that's the data-exfil window the article describes (BigQuery metadata, access lists, tenant logs, GKE cluster names, internal container image paths).

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Steam Workshop abused to spread malware via Wallpaper Engine app
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Wallpaper Engine spawning unexpected child process from Steam Workshop content directory · [LLM] AggregatorHost.dll loaded from non-System32 path (Steam credential stealer sideload) · [LLM] Known DarkKomet / Wallpaper-Engine campaign payload hash execution or write · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to Steam Workshop wallpaper campaign C2 (202.144.192.29 / 120.48.156.17 / brightly.to) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-Steam process reading Steam sentry / loginusers credential files · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Wallpaper Engine spawning unexpected child process from Steam Workshop content directory AIInstallation High
Detects Wallpaper Engine (wallpaper32.exe / wallpaper64.exe) spawning a child process whose image resides under the Steam Workshop content directory for Wallpaper Engine (app id 431960). Per Kaspersky, malicious 'application'-type wallpapers auto-execute bundled payloads at install — this is the core execution telemetry shape. Rationale: Pulls the article's specific parent binaries (Wallpaper Engine's wallpaper32.exe/wallpaper64.exe) and the Wallpaper Engine Steam Workshop app id 431960 path. Cross-checked Steam app id from public Steam Wallpaper Engine page and SteamDB. Cross-checked against: • https://store.steampowered.com/app/431960/Wallpaper_Engine/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 'application' wallpapers (system monitors, widget apps) installed by power users that the security team has not vetted
  • Wallpaper Engine self-update spawning its own installer from the Steam apps directory (parent path mismatch but similar shape)
  • Crash reporting via WerFault.exe being launched from the Workshop content folder
  • Developers testing their own Workshop submissions on dev workstations
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("WerFault.exe","WerFaultSecure.exe","dllhost.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "services.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ChildImage SHA256/MD5 and cross-reference against the article's MD5 list and threat-intel; pull the Workshop content sub-folder (the numeric id after 431960 is the Workshop item id — look it up on steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=<id> to see the wallpaper name/author). 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response or EDR network containment, kill the child process tree, remove the Workshop subscription via steam://url/CommunityFilePage/<id> when ready. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SHA256/MD5 across the fleet for other hosts with the same wallpaper, then run UC2/UC3/UC4 (AggregatorHost.dll sideload, Steam credential file access, C2 IPs) against the same DeviceId for the next 24h to surface follow-on stages.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\"
| where FileName !in~ ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe","webwallpaper32.exe","webwallpaper64.exe","conhost.exe","WerFault.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\wallpaper32.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\wallpaper64.exe"
| where NewProcessName has @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\" or CommandLine has @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\"
| where NewProcessName !endswith "\\wallpaper32.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith "\\wallpaper64.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith "\\conhost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Wallpaper Engine Spawning Child From Steam Workshop Content Directory
id: 5d7b5e4a-8a13-4d57-9e2c-31b8f1c4b2d4
description: Detects Wallpaper Engine spawning a child process whose image lives under the Wallpaper Engine Steam Workshop content folder (app id 431960).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-workshop-abused-to-spread-malware-via-wallpaper-engine-app/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wallpaper32.exe'
      - '\wallpaper64.exe'
  selection_path:
    Image|contains: '\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\'
  filter_legit:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\wallpaper32.exe'
      - '\wallpaper64.exe'
      - '\conhost.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_path and not filter_legit
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\wallpaper32.exe OR *\wallpaper64.exe OR *\Wallpaper32.exe OR *\Wallpaper64.exe) (@Image:*\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\* OR @CommandLine:*\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\*) -@Image:(*\wallpaper32.exe OR *\wallpaper64.exe OR *\conhost.exe OR *\WerFault.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/wallpaper(32|64)\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\steamapps\\\\workshop\\\\content\\\\431960\\\\", field=ImageFileName) OR regex("\\\\steamapps\\\\workshop\\\\content\\\\431960\\\\", field=CommandLine)
| NOT ImageFileName=/wallpaper(32|64)\.exe$/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/conhost\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_hash) as hashes values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe") AND (Processes.process_path="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where process_name!="wallpaper32.exe" AND process_name!="wallpaper64.exe"
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_hash) as hashes values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe") AND (Processes.process_path="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where process_name!="wallpaper32.exe" AND process_name!="wallpaper64.exe"
AggregatorHost.dll loaded from non-System32 path (Steam credential stealer sideload) AIInstallation High
Genuine AggregatorHost.dll ships in %WINDIR%\System32\. The article's payload bundles a same-named DLL outside System32 to blend in. Detects any process loading AggregatorHost.dll whose folder path is not the canonical System32 location. Rationale: Article names AggregatorHost.dll specifically as the sideloaded Steam credential stealer. Real AggregatorHost.dll is a tiny Windows .NET host stub in System32 — any other location is high-fidelity. MITRE T1574.002 mapping confirmed against attack.mitre.org. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/002/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running locally-built .NET-hosting code that names its host AggregatorHost.dll (very rare)
  • Software-deployment shares (SCCM, Intune Win32 app cache) staging the legitimate DLL under %ProgramData% before copy to System32
  • Restore/repair operations from Windows installation media mounting an offline image
  • Forensic tools or analysts running the DLL from a sandbox path during incident response
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","setup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the loaded DLL, compare SHA256/MD5 to the known-bad list in UC5, and check signature with sigcheck/Get-AuthenticodeSignature — genuine AggregatorHost.dll is Microsoft-signed; the malicious copy will be unsigned or signed by an unfamiliar publisher. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loading process, quarantine the DLL file and its parent folder (likely a Workshop subfolder under steamapps\workshop\content\431960\). 3) Hunt: enumerate all DeviceFileEvents writes of AggregatorHost.dll in the last 30 days across the fleet, pivot on InitiatingProcessFileName to find every distinct dropper, and check for outbound network connections from the loading process to the article's C2 IPs.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "AggregatorHost.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\"
     and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64\"
     and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Source =~ "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 7
| extend ImageLoaded = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[5].["#text"])
| extend ProcessImage = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[4].["#text"])
| extend ImageHashes = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[11].["#text"])
| where ImageLoaded endswith @"\AggregatorHost.dll"
| where ImageLoaded !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\"
     and ImageLoaded !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64\"
     and ImageLoaded !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessImage, ImageLoaded, ImageHashes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: a3f1c4b2-7d8e-4f9a-9b1c-2d4e5f6a7b8c
description: Detects load of AggregatorHost.dll from any folder other than the canonical System32 / SysWOW64 / WinSxS paths, a sideload technique observed in the Steam Workshop Wallpaper Engine credential-theft chain.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-workshop-abused-to-spread-malware-via-wallpaper-engine-app/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1574.002
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ImageLoaded|endswith: '\AggregatorHost.dll'
  filter_legit:
    ImageLoaded|startswith:
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\'
      - 'C:\Windows\SysWOW64\'
      - 'C:\Windows\WinSxS\'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:7 (@ImageLoaded:*\AggregatorHost.dll OR @ImageLoaded:*\aggregatorhost.dll OR @ImageLoaded:*\AGGREGATORHOST.DLL) -@ImageLoaded:(C\:\\Windows\\System32\\* OR C\:\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\* OR C\:\\Windows\\WinSxS\\*)
#event_simpleName=ClassifiedModuleLoad OR #event_simpleName=ImageHash
| TargetFileName=/\\AggregatorHost\.dll$/i
| NOT TargetFileName=/^C:\\Windows\\(System32|SysWOW64|WinSxS)\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
`sysmon` EventCode=7 ImageLoaded="*\\AggregatorHost.dll" NOT (ImageLoaded="*\\Windows\\System32\\AggregatorHost.dll" OR ImageLoaded="*\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\AggregatorHost.dll" OR ImageLoaded="*\\Windows\\WinSxS\\*\\AggregatorHost.dll") | stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Image) as loading_process values(Hashes) as dll_hashes count by host ImageLoaded User
Non-Steam process reading Steam sentry / loginusers credential files AIActions on Objectives High
Detects file reads or copies of Steam credential artefacts (ssfn* sentry files, loginusers.vdf, config.vdf) by processes that are not part of the Steam client family. The article calls out Steam account credential theft as the goal of the sideloaded AggregatorHost.dll. Rationale: ssfn* files are Steam's machine-binding sentry tokens — possession means session takeover without the password. loginusers.vdf holds the cached account list. Article explicitly states the goal is to 'search for Steam accounts on the computer and steal account credentials.' Cross-checked Steam credential artefact paths against public Steam Support documentation. Cross-checked against: • https://help.steampowered.com/en/faqs/view/65A9-CFE7-2369-A0A8 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/
ATT&CKT1555 T1539 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup utilities (Acronis, Veeam Agent, Macrium) capturing user profile data including the Steam config folder
  • AV/EDR products scanning the Steam config folder during a full filesystem sweep
  • Steam beta launcher variants or third-party Steam family-sharing tools that legitimately read ssfn files
  • Forensic acquisition tools (FTK Imager, KAPE) being run by IR or sysadmins
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backup.exe","veeamagent.exe","acronis_loader.exe","mscsweep.exe","MsMpEng.exe","kape.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName and its SHA256; if it's an unsigned binary under steamapps\workshop\content\431960\ this is almost certainly the article's stealer. Grab a copy of the file for malware analysis. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-log out the affected Steam account via Steam Account Security (deauthorize all devices), invalidate the user's Steam password and Steam Guard recovery codes, and remove the malicious wallpaper Workshop subscription. 3) Hunt: pivot on the dropper SHA256 across the fleet, query UC2 (AggregatorHost.dll sideload) and UC4 (C2 connections) for the same host, and check Steam community trade/market activity for the user's account in the last 7 days for asset theft.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
     or FolderPath has @"\Steam\config\"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^(loginusers\.vdf|config\.vdf|ssfn[0-9]+)$"
     or FolderPath has @"\Steam\config\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("steam.exe","steamservice.exe","steamwebhelper.exe","gameoverlayui.exe","streaming_client.exe","steamerrorreporter.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Steam\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(loginusers\.vdf|config\.vdf|ssfn[0-9]+)$"
   or TargetFilePath has @"\Steam\config\"
| where not (ActingProcessName has_any ("steam.exe","steamservice.exe","steamwebhelper.exe","gameoverlayui.exe","streaming_client.exe","steamerrorreporter.exe"))
| where not (ActingProcessCommandLine has @"\Steam\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Steam Process Accessing Steam Credential Artefacts
id: 7b9c1d2e-3f4a-5b6c-7d8e-9f0a1b2c3d4e
description: Detects file access to Steam sentry (ssfn*), loginusers.vdf, or config.vdf by processes outside the Steam client family — the credential-theft step of the Steam Workshop Wallpaper Engine campaign.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-workshop-abused-to-spread-malware-via-wallpaper-engine-app/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1555
  - attack.t1539
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_files:
    TargetFilename|re: '(?i)\\(loginusers\.vdf|config\.vdf|ssfn[0-9]+)$'
  filter_steam:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\steam.exe'
      - '\steamservice.exe'
      - '\steamwebhelper.exe'
      - '\gameoverlayui.exe'
      - '\streaming_client.exe'
      - '\steamerrorreporter.exe'
  condition: selection_files and not filter_steam
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\loginusers.vdf OR @TargetFilename:*\LoginUsers.vdf OR @TargetFilename:*\config.vdf OR @TargetFilename:*\Config.vdf OR @TargetFilename:*\ssfn* OR @TargetFilename:*\Steam\config\*) -@Image:(*\steam.exe OR *\Steam.exe OR *\steamservice.exe OR *\steamwebhelper.exe OR *\gameoverlayui.exe OR *\GameOverlayUI.exe OR *\streaming_client.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo OR #event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(\\loginusers\.vdf|\\config\.vdf|\\ssfn[0-9]+|\\Steam\\config\\)/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(steam|steamservice|steamwebhelper|gameoverlayui|streaming_client|steamerrorreporter)\.exe$/i
| NOT regex("\\\\Steam\\\\", field=ContextImageFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path values(Filesystem.process_name) as process from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="loginusers.vdf" OR Filesystem.file_name="config.vdf" OR Filesystem.file_name="ssfn*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)^(steam|steamservice|steamwebhelper|gameoverlayui|streaming_client)\.exe$")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path values(Filesystem.process_name) as process from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="loginusers.vdf" OR Filesystem.file_name="config.vdf" OR Filesystem.file_name="ssfn*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)^(steam|steamservice|steamwebhelper|gameoverlayui|streaming_client)\.exe$")
Outbound connection to Steam Workshop wallpaper campaign C2 (202.144.192.29 / 120.48.156.17 / brightly.to) AICommand & Control High
Network beacon to the three article-named C2 endpoints used by the DarkKomet backdoor / AggregatorHost stealer / Lumma / Vidar / RanEngine payloads delivered through malicious Wallpaper Engine wallpapers. Any internal host contacting these is high-confidence compromise. Rationale: All three indicators are named directly in the kill-chain reconstruction for the same campaign and tied to multiple distinct payload families (DarkKomet, AggregatorHost, Lumma, Vidar, RanEngine). No second-source corroboration yet (campaign just published), so confidence relies on the Kaspersky attribution; treat any internal hit as a confirmed-compromise pivot.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed validation traffic from a security tool (e.g. analyst sandbox detonation hitting the C2)
  • Researcher VM intentionally browsing brightly.to for analysis
  • Shared-hosting provider parking the IP on an unrelated benign domain (verify reverse DNS)
  • Outbound proxy / SASE service health-checking a blocklisted URL
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","falcon-sensor.exe","sentinelagent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which internal hosts connected and which user/process initiated; pull InitiatingProcessFileName & InitiatingProcessFolderPath — if process lives under steamapps\workshop\content\431960\ this is the article's chain. 2) Contain: block 202.144.192.29, 120.48.156.17, and *.brightly.to at egress firewall + DNS sinkhole; isolate the originating hosts via EDR network containment; force-revoke Steam Guard tokens and reset Steam passwords for affected users. 3) Hunt: run UC1/UC2/UC3 across the same DeviceId for the previous 30 days, search DeviceFileEvents for the hashes in UC5, and pivot from the originating process SHA256 across the fleet to find any other host with the same dropper.
let C2_IPs = dynamic(["202.144.192.29","120.48.156.17"]);
let C2_Domains = dynamic(["brightly.to"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2_IPs)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (C2_Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2_IPs = dynamic(["202.144.192.29","120.48.156.17"]);
let C2_Domains = dynamic(["brightly.to"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImNetworkSession
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DstIpAddr in (C2_IPs) or DstHostname in~ (C2_Domains) or Url has_any (C2_Domains)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=SrcUsername, Process=tostring(parse_json("")), RemoteIP=DstIpAddr, RemoteUrl=coalesce(DstHostname, Url)),
    (ImDnsActivity
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DnsQuery in~ (C2_Domains)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=SrcUsername, Process="", RemoteIP="", RemoteUrl=DnsQuery),
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DestinationIP in (C2_IPs) or RequestURL has_any (C2_Domains) or DestinationDnsDomain has_any (C2_Domains)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, User=SourceUserName, Process=DestinationProcessName, RemoteIP=DestinationIP, RemoteUrl=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationDnsDomain))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known DarkKomet / Wallpaper-Engine campaign payload hash execution or write AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution or file-write of any of the 13 article-named MD5s tied to the malicious wallpaper bundles (DarkKomet droppers, AggregatorHost.dll variants, Lumma/Vidar/RanEngine stages). Pure IOC hunt; will catch any host that downloaded a known-bad Workshop package even if behaviour-based UCs missed it. Rationale: All 13 MD5s are taken verbatim from the article's pre-extracted IOC bundle covering the DarkKomet droppers and AggregatorHost.dll sideload payloads. 90-day lookback because some Workshop subscriptions sit on disk for weeks before installation/launch.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox or research VM in the fleet legitimately running known-bad samples
  • EDR / SOAR auto-detonation pipeline (e.g. ANY.RUN connector) leaving sample artefacts on a SOC host
  • Threat-intel vendor agent caching a sample for offline scanning
  • Old quarantine restore on an analyst workstation pulling a sample for reverse engineering
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm hit isn't an analyst sandbox; pull DeviceName, FolderPath, parent process and timeline of the file write — chase upstream to find the wallpaper Workshop item id (the path under steamapps\workshop\content\431960\<id>\). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any running process matching the hash, quarantine the file system-wide via Defender Indicator (FileHash → BlockAndRemediate), push the 13 hashes to corporate AV/EDR blocklists. 3) Hunt: run UC4 (C2 IPs) and UC3 (Steam credential file access) against the affected host for the last 90 days; submit the Workshop item id (and author Steam ID) to Valve security via steamcommunity.com/dev for takedown; query CrowdStrike / Defender across the fleet for any other host with these MD5s on disk even without execution.
let BadMD5 = dynamic(["95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068","af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a","c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf","d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da","8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854","b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09","ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1","20965254e29104986e11939decd39549","18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883","0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d","5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355","fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6","74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
        | where MD5 in (BadMD5) or InitiatingProcessMD5 in (BadMD5)
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source="Process", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath),
    (DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
        | where MD5 in (BadMD5)
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="FileWrite", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath),
    (DeviceImageLoadEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
        | where MD5 in (BadMD5)
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="DllLoad", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath)
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadMD5 = dynamic(["95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068","af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a","c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf","d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da","8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854","b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09","ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1","20965254e29104986e11939decd39549","18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883","0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d","5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355","fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6","74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
        | where MD5 in (BadMD5)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, Source="Process", FileName=TargetProcessName, CommandLine=TargetProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256),
    (ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
        | where TargetFileMD5 in (BadMD5) or Hash in (BadMD5)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, Source="FileEvent", FileName=TargetFileName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, MD5=TargetFileMD5, SHA256=TargetFileSHA256),
    (SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where FileHash has_any (BadMD5)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, User=SubjectUserName, Source="4688", FileName=NewProcessName, CommandLine=CommandLine, MD5=FileHash, SHA256="")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80") or SHA1 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80") or MD5 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80") or SHA1 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80") or MD5 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ClickFix Campaigns Expand Malware Delivery With New Loaders and Fake Update Lures

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 18 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged multiple ClickFix campaigns that deliver three malware loaders called BabaDeda Loader, Lorem Ipsum Loader, and Potemkin, per independent reports from Morphisec, BlueVoyant, and Huntress, respectively. Attacks involving BabaDeda Loader, observed in April 2026, have targeted education and financial organizations. "Earlier BabaDeda activity was known for
