Langflow runtime writing executable or staging file to /tmp, /var/tmp, or /dev/shm AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Langflow python process writing files to common staging directories (/tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm) — the PoC for CVE-2026-48519 literally drops `/tmp/pwned`, and real-world Langflow exploitation campaigns drop crypto miners and reverse-shell binaries to these locations. Rationale: Anchors on the article's PoC payload exactly: `touch /tmp/pwned`. Sysdig and JFrog reporting on the related CVE-2026-33017 in-the-wild exploitation shows attackers drop XMRig miners, reverse-shell ELFs, and Flodrix botnet stagers into /tmp and /dev/shm from the langflow runtime. The exclusion list filters Python's normal tempfile noise (tmpXXXX, pip-*, pytest-*, .pyc) so true positives surface. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-33017-how-attackers-compromised-langflow-ai-pipelines-in-20-hours • https://research.jfrog.com/post/langflow-latest-version-was-not-fixed/ • https://www.runzero.com/blog/langflow/
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow legitimate caching of LangChain artifacts to /tmp
  • Custom Langflow component using tempfile module for intermediate file output
  • Ray/serve framework writing object-store spill files (mostly excluded by ray_ prefix)
  • HuggingFace model downloader caching tokenizer files under TMPDIR=/tmp
Suppression filter
| where TargetFileName !endswith ".json" and TargetFileName !endswith ".log" and TargetFileSize > 100
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Hash each suspect file (sha256sum) and check VirusTotal / internal repute. Read the file (`file`, `strings`, `xxd` first 256 bytes) — ELF magic 7f454c46 = binary payload, #!/bin/sh = shell script. Check executable bit. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the file via EDR; kill the langflow worker PID that wrote it; isolate host network if file is unknown-bad. Step 3 (hunt): If file is a known miner/RAT, pivot on its file hash org-wide across DeviceFileEvents and DeviceProcessEvents. Check egress for the C2 IPs from any process. Correlate with UC1 to find the exploit POST that delivered the dropper.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12","uvicorn","gunicorn")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow","uvicorn langflow","langflow.main")
| where FolderPath startswith "/tmp/"
    or FolderPath startswith "/var/tmp/"
    or FolderPath startswith "/dev/shm/"
| where FileName !startswith "tmp"
    and FileName !startswith "pip-"
    and FileName !startswith "pytest-"
    and FileName !endswith ".pyc"
    and FileName !startswith "ray_"
    and FileName !startswith ".com.google"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileCreate","FileModified")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","uvicorn","gunicorn")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow","uvicorn langflow","langflow.main")
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/tmp/"
    or TargetFilePath startswith "/var/tmp/"
    or TargetFilePath startswith "/dev/shm/"
| where TargetFileName !startswith "tmp"
    and TargetFileName !startswith "pip-"
    and TargetFileName !startswith "pytest-"
    and TargetFileName !endswith ".pyc"
    and TargetFileName !startswith "ray_"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(PATH OR SYSCALL) (@process.name:(python OR python3 OR python3.10 OR python3.11 OR python3.12 OR uvicorn OR gunicorn) OR @process.command_line:*langflow*) (@file.path:("/tmp/*" OR "/var/tmp/*" OR "/dev/shm/*")) -@file.name:(tmp* OR pip-* OR pytest-* OR *.pyc OR ray_*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/\/(python|python3|python3\.\d+|uvicorn|gunicorn)$/i OR regex("langflow", field=ContextImageFileName) OR regex("langflow", field=CommandLine)
| TargetFileName=/^\/(tmp|var\/tmp|dev\/shm)\//i
| NOT (TargetFileName=/\/(tmp[A-Za-z0-9]+|pip-|pytest-|ray_)/i OR TargetFileName=/\.pyc$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count(as=WriteCount))
| sort(field=WriteCount, order=desc)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count, values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths, values(Filesystem.file_name) as files, min(_time) as first_seen from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name IN ("python","python3","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12","uvicorn") OR Filesystem.process_path="*langflow*") AND Filesystem.action="created" AND (Filesystem.file_path="/tmp/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/var/tmp/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/dev/shm/*") by host, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where NOT match(file_name, "^(tmp[A-Za-z0-9]+|pip-|pytest-|\\.pyc$|ray_)") | sort - first_seen
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths, values(Filesystem.file_name) as files, min(_time) as first_seen from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name IN ("python","python3","python3.10","python3.11","python3.12","uvicorn") OR Filesystem.process_path="*langflow*") AND Filesystem.action="created" AND (Filesystem.file_path="/tmp/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/var/tmp/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="/dev/shm/*") by host, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where NOT match(file_name, "^(tmp[A-Za-z0-9]+|pip-|pytest-|\\.pyc$|ray_)") | sort - first_seen
Burst of HTTP 4xx/5xx responses to /api/v1/build_public_tmp from single source (CVE-2026-48519 scanner) AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces hosts being scanned for CVE-2026-48519 — exploit kits and Nuclei templates probe /api/v1/build_public_tmp with malformed flow payloads before landing a successful POST. A burst of error responses to this specific endpoint from one source IP is a strong reconnaissance signal that precedes successful RCE. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact endpoint path. Exploit kits for CVE-2026-33017 (the publicly-known sibling) probe with a handful of malformed payloads before a successful POST — Sysdig reported first in-the-wild exploitation within 20 hours of disclosure, almost always preceded by 4xx scanner bursts. Threshold of 5 errors / 10 min from one source separates targeted scanning from incidental client errors. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-33017-how-attackers-compromised-langflow-ai-pipelines-in-20-hours • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4151203/attackers-exploit-critical-langflow-rce-within-hours-as-cisa-sounds-alarm.html • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/hackers-exploit-critical-langflow/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Tenable, Qualys, Rapid7) running authenticated checks against Langflow
  • DAST tool (Burp, ZAP) crawling Langflow during a security assessment
  • Misconfigured legitimate client retrying with bad flow ID after an admin renames a public flow
  • Health-probe tool hitting build_public_tmp with empty body (would get 422)
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<internal-scanner-cidr>","<pentest-jumpbox-ips>","<healthcheck-ips>"]))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the source IP — internal scanner range, known pentest jumpbox, or external? Check whether any request from that source got a 200 (successful exploitation, escalate immediately to UC1 + UC2 hunt). Step 2 (contain): If external and no 200s yet — add source IP to perimeter blocklist; alert app owner. If 200 observed — treat as confirmed compromise; isolate the Langflow host. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all Langflow instances org-wide for the same source IP touching /api/v1/build_public_tmp. Audit which flows are configured as public (Shareable Playground) — recommend disabling Shareable Playground until upgrade to Langflow >1.9.1.
let WindowMin = 10m;
let ErrorBurstThreshold = 5;
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where RequestURL has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
     | extend StatusCode = toint(coalesce(tostring(EventOutcome), DeviceCustomString1))
     | where StatusCode >= 400
     | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestURL, StatusCode, UA=RequestClientApplication),
  (W3CIISLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where csUriStem startswith "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
     | where scStatus >= 400
     | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP=cIP, DestinationIP=Computer, RequestURL=csUriStem, StatusCode=scStatus, UA=csUserAgent),
  (AppServiceHTTPLogs
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where CsUriStem startswith "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
     | where ScStatus >= 400
     | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP=CIp, DestinationIP=CsHost, RequestURL=CsUriStem, StatusCode=ScStatus, UA=UserAgent)
| summarize ErrorCount=count(),
            DistinctStatus=make_set(StatusCode,10),
            UserAgents=make_set(UA,5),
            FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated)
            by SourceIP, DestinationIP, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMin)
| where ErrorCount >= ErrorBurstThreshold
| order by ErrorCount desc
(source:(nginx.access OR apache.access OR http OR aws.alb OR cloudflare)) @http.url_details.path:*build_public_tmp* (@http.status_code:>=400)
# log group: /aws/applicationelb/<your-langflow-alb> (or any HTTP access-log group fronting Langflow)
fields @timestamp, client_ip, request_url, request_verb, target_status_code, user_agent
| filter request_url like /\/api\/v1\/build_public_tmp/
  and target_status_code >= 400
| stats count() as error_count,
        count_distinct(request_url) as distinct_paths,
        earliest(@timestamp) as first_seen,
        latest(@timestamp) as last_seen,
        count_distinct(user_agent) as ua_count
  by client_ip, bin(10m)
| filter error_count >= 5
| sort error_count desc
| limit 100
WEB

| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Web.url) as distinct_urls, values(Web.status) as status_codes, values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents, min(_time) as first_seen, max(_time) as last_seen from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/api/v1/build_public_tmp*" Web.status>=400 by Web.src, Web.dest, bin(_time, span=10m) | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count >= 5 | eval duration_sec = last_seen - first_seen | sort - count

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;

| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

2026-06-16 7 use cases 1 technique 4 kill-chain phases detected

NTFS junction creation via cmd.exe mklink /J AIInstallation High
Detects the foundational primitive of the GhostTree EDR-evasion technique: a user-mode process invoking cmd.exe with `mklink /J` to create an NTFS directory junction. The article confirms only write permissions are needed (no admin) and that the same syntax is used to build the recursive Parent\Child loop. Rationale: Anchors on the exact two-token combination from Code Block 1 (`mklink /J`) inside cmd.exe — the verbatim invocation the article gives as the GhostBranch/GhostTree primitive. Legit non-admin junction creation is rare outside of WSL/dev setup, making this a high-fidelity signal even before correlating multiple events.
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WSL/Docker Desktop install routines creating junctions under %LOCALAPPDATA%
  • Veeam, Acronis or other backup tooling staging shadow-copy mount points via mklink
  • Developer scripts symlinking node_modules or build output between projects
  • Group Policy folder-redirection scripts setting up profile junctions
  • Windows In-place upgrade / setup leaving mklink invocations in setupact context
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("wsl.exe", "docker.exe", "setup.exe", "msiexec.exe", "veeam.backup.shell.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\System32\" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("services.exe", "trustedinstaller.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full junction target path from CommandLine and inspect with `fsutil reparsepoint query <path>` and `dir /AL <parent>` — confirm whether the link target points to its own parent or ancestor (the GhostTree shape). Check parent process: if it's explorer.exe / a shell launched from a user-clicked .lnk or unsigned .bat, treat as malicious. Step 2 (contain): On the affected host, enumerate the junction target with `fsutil reparsepoint delete <path>` to break the loop, then run a Defender full scan of the previously-unscannable parent folder. Isolate host if any binaries are dropped alongside the junction. Step 3 (hunt): Across the fleet, search DeviceFileEvents for executable writes into the same parent folder within +/- 60 minutes of the junction creation, and pivot on the AccountName for other anomalous cmd.exe invocations in the last 7 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "mklink" and ProcessCommandLine has "/J"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\cmd.exe"
| where CommandLine has "mklink" and CommandLine has "/J"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: NTFS Junction Creation via cmd.exe mklink /J
id: 9f2c4d8a-1b3e-4a5f-8c7d-2e9b6f1a4d5c
description: Detects creation of NTFS directory junctions via cmd's mklink /J - the primary primitive used by the GhostTree EDR-evasion technique to build recursive directory loops that hang folder scans.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1564.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\cmd.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'mklink'
      - '/J'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\Cmd.exe) @CommandLine:(*mklink* OR *MKLINK*) @CommandLine:(*"/J"* OR *"/j"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\cmd\.exe$/i
| regex("mklink", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| regex("/J\\b", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Processes.process) as cmdline, values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" Processes.process="*mklink*" Processes.process="* /J *" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Processes.process) as cmdline, values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" Processes.process="*mklink*" Processes.process="* /J *" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
NTFS reparse point manipulation via fsutil reparsepoint AIInstallation High
Detects the alternate API used to create or modify NTFS reparse points: `fsutil.exe reparsepoint`. GhostTree only needs a junction-style reparse point, and fsutil is the LOLBin path an attacker uses when mklink is blocked or audited. Pairs with the mklink detection to close the obvious bypass. Rationale: fsutil reparsepoint is the documented Windows API for the exact same NTFS reparse-point primitive the article describes. Attackers blocked from cmd's mklink will pivot here. Selecting on the `create`/`set` subcommands filters out the noisier read-only `query` usage that sysadmins run for troubleshooting.
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Storage admin running fsutil reparsepoint to repair a broken mount point
  • Backup software setting reparse points for VSS / dedup tags
  • Windows servicing stack (DISM / TrustedInstaller) tagging WinSxS folders
  • Container runtime tooling configuring layer mount reparse points
  • IT scripts converting roaming-profile junctions during migrations
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("trustedinstaller.exe", "dism.exe", "setup.exe", "veeam.backup.shell.exe", "dedupproc.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel != "System" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("services.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the full CommandLine and the target path; query the resulting reparse point with `fsutil reparsepoint query <path>` to determine reparse tag (0xA0000003 = mount point/junction) and the substitute path. If the substitute path resolves to the parent or an ancestor of the link itself, treat as confirmed GhostTree. Step 2 (contain): Delete the reparse attribute with `fsutil reparsepoint delete <path>`, then immediately scan the containing folder with Defender / EDR full file scan. Preserve a forensic copy of any executables that emerge from the previously-unscannable directory. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the AccountName and SubjectLogonId to find every fsutil and cmd.exe invocation in the last 30 days; specifically look for chained fsutil+mklink calls and for executable drops (DeviceFileEvents FileCreated where FolderPath = junction parent) within the same logon session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "fsutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "reparsepoint"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("create", "set")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\fsutil.exe"
| where CommandLine has "reparsepoint"
| where CommandLine has_any ("create", "set")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: NTFS Reparse Point Creation via fsutil

source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\fsutil.exe OR *\\FSUTIL.EXE OR *\\Fsutil.exe) @CommandLine:*reparsepoint* @CommandLine:(*create* OR *CREATE* OR *set* OR *SET*)

GhostTree pattern: multiple NTFS junctions created under same parent within minutes AIInstallation High
Detects the GhostTree giveaway: a single user/host issuing 2+ `mklink /J` commands inside a short window, which is the signature of building the binary-tree of `Child1`/`Child2` (or `P`/`B`) junctions the article describes. A single junction is benign; a burst of them under one user session is the recursive loop being constructed. Rationale: GhostBranch only needs one junction; GhostTree explicitly requires multiple (the article's Child1+Child2, or P+B examples). A 10-minute bucket with >=2 mklink /J invocations from the same user/host is the cleanest temporal signature of the technique being staged rather than a one-off legitimate junction. The bin/summarize structure stays inside canonical DeviceProcessEvents columns (DeviceName, AccountName, Timestamp) — no extracted-path columns required.
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WSL or Docker install creating multiple junctions during first-run setup
  • Developer batch script setting up multiple symlinked module directories in one go
  • Migration tool batch-creating junctions for legacy app path compatibility
  • Backup product staging multiple VSS mount-point junctions during snapshot prep
  • Group Policy logon script redirecting several profile folders via junction
Suppression filter
| where ParentProc !in~ ("wsl.exe", "docker.exe", "setup.exe", "msiexec.exe", "veeam.backup.shell.exe", "dism.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each junction created in the burst, run `fsutil reparsepoint query <path>` and `dir /AL <parent>` to map the link graph. If any junction's substitute path resolves to its own parent or ancestor, the recursive loop is confirmed and the containing folder is unscannable. Step 2 (contain): Delete each junction in the cluster with `fsutil reparsepoint delete <path>` (or `rmdir` — do NOT use `rd /s` which can follow the loop). Then isolate the host and trigger a full EDR scan of the now-flat parent directory. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the SubjectLogonId of the burst — pull every DeviceFileEvents FileCreated under that AccountName in +/- 4 hours, focusing on .exe/.dll/.ps1 writes that landed in the freed parent folder. Cross-check DeviceProcessEvents for any executable launched FROM that parent path post-junction-creation (the payload that was being hidden).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "mklink" and ProcessCommandLine has "/J"
| summarize JunctionCount = count(),
            SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine),
            ParentProc = any(InitiatingProcessFileName),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
          by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where JunctionCount >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\cmd.exe"
| where CommandLine has "mklink" and CommandLine has "/J"
| summarize JunctionCount = count(),
            SampleCmd = any(CommandLine),
            ParentProc = any(ParentProcessName),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by Computer, SubjectUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where JunctionCount >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\Cmd.exe) @CommandLine:(*mklink* OR *MKLINK*) @CommandLine:(*"/J"* OR *"/j"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\cmd\.exe$/i
| regex("mklink", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| regex("/J\\b", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| bucket(span=10m, field=@timestamp)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, _bucket], function=count(as=JunctionCount))
| JunctionCount >= 2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as JunctionCount, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Processes.process) as SampleCmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" Processes.process="*mklink*" Processes.process="* /J *" by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where JunctionCount >= 2 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count as JunctionCount, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Processes.process) as SampleCmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="cmd.exe" Processes.process="*mklink*" Processes.process="* /J *" by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where JunctionCount >= 2 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",

SecurityEvent

| where Account !endswith "$"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hackers Weaponize Microsoft Teams Relay to Hide Ransomware Traffic

Cyber Security News
2026-06-16 9 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Hackers are increasingly abusing trusted cloud services to evade detection, and a newly uncovered campaign demonstrates how Microsoft Teams infrastructure can be weaponized to hide malicious traffic. According to&#160;the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, a new Go-based remote access Trojan (RAT) named Backdoor.TURN leverages Microsoft Teams TURN relay servers to disguise command-and-control (C2) communications as legitimate [&#8230;] The post Hackers Weaponize Microsoft Teams Relay to Hide Ransomware Traffic appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession

| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

| where files > 200

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-52271", "CVE-2025-61155", "CVE-2025-1055")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-52271", "CVE-2025-61155", "CVE-2025-1055")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2023-52271", "CVE-2025-61155", "CVE-2025-1055")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2023-52271", "CVE-2025-61155", "CVE-2025-1055")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

let BadHashes = dynamic(["82b37a92589dfd4d67ca87eb9e52ac8e682e8e60d2211f59074cd5ccc693013b", "821da79d727351dd67ce5df7950e9a3de6647a3cf474bb3a093f67507fed92a6", "b6628d201c2a68d2a3de2a87de7a5acfe21b101a97928e1c8d5c82102d967383", "ce66b8221446c9b6d83f0ce6382f430e519601641e5daaaf1ca7a8a8806cb0b0", "f174c19902523dcf005fa044b6598403a5e5c0a5982398d1bc0dcc5ec1cd351b", "142bac0e2148e0d47891b6cd7311195c4acbe33b700fad54a201c52a2bc46219", "8395b621bb4415090f232c59fc41d24ea41a519b58eabe512f3ae7d2fdf049a3", "9335f61f8ad276d94455c5b6876fea48152c3cea759f2598c8108ee461fa5759", "cd078957167e1af4de39aecdb981cd14156fa81d5a9c6ac51e74ae5b6199a12a", "b16e217cdca19e00c1b68bdfb28ead53b20adeabd6edcd91542f9fbf48942877", "d20a3c928761fe00ac522eeb474612b5804cd9108453ea8591106d5d4428428e", "8284c8676cc22c4b2e66826ac16986da7ddecba1f2776b16771be17bfdc45dc2", "65ab49119c845801f29a57e8aa177146b2ffbd289d4278109b146f933380f951", "6bbf10bcbef7ac5102b54c81137859891a3802dbacd888be90f990d50e18b0b4", "252a8bb2eb9c96c5e6cc7cab822e2ed0d508032f9350351221781684e86c03ab", "8a4033425d36cd99fe23e6faef9764fbf555f362ebdb5b72379342fbbe4c5531", "e45b18c93d187aac5c4486f57483bc87580e15def82a312bfb377ff16eb96b22", "087f002df0a02c8c74f3ba5cd99cf29fb9efff38bf57b3d808e34a5dd4200dd2", "048e18416177de2ead251abdf4d89837f6807c6aba4d5b1debe49adfdecbf05c", "6f9fbe29f8cc2788e2bc9d631e0eea2a8e9837076837b55838005a0e654f0a9e", "d0da2832ae1e13a98f7ce7e33a66c1b0d9797b81f69ece134e4462ea55ac923e", "aea26980059ef2ad11e99556a4edfa1f8ec769fa9f06aa573b81bedf319954b5"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New Rokarolla Android Malware Steals PINs, SMS Codes, and Crypto Wallet Funds

The Hacker News
2026-06-16 5 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Security researchers at&nbsp;Zimperium's zLabs&nbsp;have documented a new Android banking trojan, Rokarolla, that targets 217 banking and cryptocurrency apps and packs 137 remote commands. Together, they give an operator near-total control of an infected phone: it lifts lock-screen PINs, reads and sends SMS, rewrites the clipboard to redirect crypto payments, and switches off Google Play

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Rokarolla Android banking trojan C2 contact — beralisvc.info · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
Rokarolla Android banking trojan C2 contact — beralisvc.info AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS resolution or HTTP(S) network traffic to beralisvc.info, the named command-and-control domain for the Rokarolla Android banking trojan documented by Zimperium zLabs in June 2026. The malware is named after this C2 family; any successful resolution from a managed mobile device, BYOD on corporate Wi-Fi, or corporate egress path is a near-certain indicator of an infected Android device performing overlay-credential exfiltration, SMS OTP theft, or accessibility-driven screenshot upload. Rationale: Anchored on the single hard IOC the article names — the C2 domain beralisvc.info — which the malware family is itself named after (Zimperium named it after the C2 servers). Behavioral TTPs in the article (Accessibility abuse, default-SMS-app hijack, overlay credential theft, screenshot-via-Accessibility exfiltration) require mobile-EDR-specific telemetry that isn't part of the standard Defender/Sentinel/Falcon/Datadog schemas in this prompt, so additional UCs would either restate this network IOC or hallucinate column names. One sharp detection beats five generic mobile templates. Cross-checked against The Hacker News, Infosecurity Magazine, and HackRead — all three independent write-ups attribute the campaign to Zimperium zLabs and confirm the C2-naming convention. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-rokarolla-android-malware-steals.html • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/rokarolla-android-banking-trojan/ • https://hackread.com/rokarolla-android-trojan-crypto-and-banking-apps/ • https://zimperium.com/blog/android-bankers-4-campaigns-in-a-row
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1437.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analysis sandbox / detonation VM resolving the IOC after a sample upload
  • Threat intel platform (MISP, OpenCTI, ThreatConnect) running automated enrichment lookups against the published IOC
  • Browser link-unfurling or preview services automatically fetching domain context when SOC analysts share the article in chat
  • SOC engineer manually pinging or curl-checking the domain during this very investigation
  • Mobile DFIR lab triaging a captured device with live C2 still active
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("malware-sandbox-01","ti-detonation-vm","sandbox-android-01","misp-enrichment-host") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("curl.exe","curl","wget.exe","wget","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","python.exe","python3") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "misp" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "opencti"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceInfo (OSPlatform, JoinType, LoggedOnUsers) for the resolving device. If Android, identify owner via MDM/Intune and confirm BYOD vs corporate-owned. If Windows/Linux or a known analyst workstation, validate against TI-sandbox/IR-tooling allowlist before escalating. Capture the InitiatingProcessFileName — on Android Defender this surfaces the offending package name. 2) Contain: for confirmed end-user mobile infections, issue Intune retire-and-wipe (factory reset is required; reinstall-only leaves the dropper). Force credential rotation for every banking, crypto-exchange, wallet, email, and SSO account ever used on the device. Sinkhole beralisvc.info and *.beralisvc.info at the corporate resolver and egress firewall. Notify the user's bank fraud team — SMS-OTP capture means recent transactions may be attacker-initiated. 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for the prior 14 days for other newly-resolved low-reputation .info/.top/.xyz domains (fallback C2), elevated counts of 
let C2Domains = dynamic(["beralisvc.info"]);
let Lookback = 14d;
union isfuzzy=true
( DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains)
       or RemoteUrl endswith ".beralisvc.info"
  | extend Source = "DeviceNetworkEvents", QueryOrUrl = RemoteUrl
  | project Timestamp, Source, DeviceName, DeviceId, QueryOrUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName ),
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains)
       or RemoteUrl endswith ".beralisvc.info"
  | extend Source = "DeviceEvents/DnsQueryResponse", QueryOrUrl = RemoteUrl
  | project Timestamp, Source, DeviceName, DeviceId, QueryOrUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort = toint(0),
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName = AccountName )
| join kind=leftouter ( DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, JoinType, LoggedOnUsers) by DeviceId ) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, Source, DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, JoinType, LoggedOnUsers,
          QueryOrUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domains = dynamic(["beralisvc.info"]);
let Lookback = 14d;
union isfuzzy=true
( DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
  | where Name has_any (C2Domains) or Name endswith ".beralisvc.info"
  | extend Source = "DnsEvents", QueryName = Name, ClientHost = Computer, Client = ClientIP
  | project TimeGenerated, Source, ClientHost, Client, QueryName, QueryType ),
( ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (C2Domains) or DnsQuery endswith ".beralisvc.info"
  | extend Source = "ImDnsActivity", QueryName = DnsQuery, ClientHost = DvcHostname, Client = SrcIpAddr, QueryType = DnsQueryTypeName
  | project TimeGenerated, Source, ClientHost, Client, QueryName, QueryType ),
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
  | where DestinationHostName has_any (C2Domains)
       or DestinationHostName endswith ".beralisvc.info"
       or RequestURL has "beralisvc.info"
  | extend Source = "CommonSecurityLog", QueryName = coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), ClientHost = SourceHostName, Client = SourceIP, QueryType = tostring(DestinationPort)
  | project TimeGenerated, Source, ClientHost, Client, QueryName, QueryType )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Rokarolla Android Banking Trojan C2 Domain Resolution (beralisvc.info)
id: 9b3c6f5d-1e7a-4b2c-8d9f-5a3e1c8b7d2f
description: Detects DNS resolution requests for beralisvc.info, the named command-and-control domain of the Rokarolla Android banking trojan reported by Zimperium zLabs in June 2026. The malware family is named after this C2 cluster and any resolution from a managed device strongly indicates an infected Android endpoint.
references:
    - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-rokarolla-android-malware-steals.html
    - https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/rokarolla-android-banking-trojan/
    - https://hackread.com/rokarolla-android-trojan-crypto-and-banking-apps/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
    - attack.t1071.001
    - attack.t1071.004
    - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
    category: dns
detection:
    selection_exact:
        query: 'beralisvc.info'
    selection_sub:
        query|endswith: '.beralisvc.info'
    condition: selection_exact or selection_sub
falsepositives:
    - Malware analysis sandbox detonating the sample
    - Threat intel enrichment tooling pre-resolving published IOCs
level: high
(@dns.question.name:(*beralisvc.info OR *.beralisvc.info OR *BERALISVC.INFO) OR @network.destination.domain:(*beralisvc.info OR *BERALISVC.INFO) OR @http.url:*beralisvc.info OR @url.domain:*beralisvc.info) AND -source:vulnerability_management
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\.)beralisvc\.info$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=[count(as=Hits), min(@timestamp, as=FirstSeen), max(@timestamp, as=LastSeen)])

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium

ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

CISA warns of another cPanel plugin flaw exploited in attacks

BleepingComputer
2026-06-16 5 use cases 0 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has given U.S. government agencies three days to secure their servers against an actively exploited vulnerability (CVE-2026-54420) in the LiteSpeed cPanel user-end plugin. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] cPanel LiteSpeed Plugin Exploit Endpoint Hit (CVE-2026-54420 / CVE-2026-48172)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Symlink to cPanel/LiteSpeed Root-Owned Paths from Low-Privilege User (CageFS Escape) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — CISA warns of another cPanel plugin flaw exploited in attacks
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Root Shell or Persistence Tool Spawned by lsws/cpanel Plugin Parent (Post-Exploit)
cPanel LiteSpeed Plugin Exploit Endpoint Hit (CVE-2026-54420 / CVE-2026-48172) AIExploitation High
Detects the LiteSpeed-published exploitation signature for the cPanel user-end plugin UNIX symlink-following vulnerability — requests calling the generateEcCert or packageUserSize JSON API functions, or cert_action_entry records referencing geneccert. These are the exact strings LiteSpeed told operators to grep for in /usr/local/cpanel/logs and /var/cpanel/logs. Rationale: Strings are taken verbatim from the LiteSpeed-published vulnerability check grep regex in the article: 'cpanel_jsonapi_func=(generateEcCert|packageUserSize)|cert_action_entry .*geneccert'. The vendor itself states any output is presumptive evidence of exploitation. Defender XDR / Falcon FDR don't ingest cPanel app logs natively, so endpoint-tier queries are omitted; CloudWatch is irrelevant unless logs are shipped to AWS — left empty.
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate cPanel users with patched plugin (>= 2.4.8) running SSL/Let's Encrypt certificate-generation workflows — the same API endpoint is exercised
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys) probing for the CVE that mirror the exploit URL
  • Operator-run forensic grep against the same log paths echoing the strings into shell history that gets shipped to SIEM
  • Backup/log-shipping retries replaying historic log lines that contain the strings from a prior incident
  • cPanel plugin self-test suites that exercise the same JSON API endpoints during upgrade
Suppression filter
// Suppress patched hosts and known scanner sources
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert", "cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize")
   or SyslogMessage matches regex @"cert_action_entry\s+.*geneccert"
| where Computer !in (dynamic(["<patched-hosts-watchlist>"]))
| where not(SyslogMessage has_any ("<scanner-ip-allowlist>"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the cPanel host's LiteSpeed user-end plugin version — anything < 2.4.8 plus a hit on these strings is presumptive compromise. Pull the requesting src IP, requesting cPanel user account, and exact URI from the access log; cross-reference against known scanner IP allowlists. Step 2 (contain): Force-update the LiteSpeed plugin to 2.4.8+ across all shared-hosting nodes, suspend the implicated cPanel user account, rotate that user's FTP/SSH/cPanel credentials, and snapshot the host for forensics. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC2/UC3 — search the same host's process telemetry for `ln -s` into /usr/local/lsws or /usr/local/cpanel from the suspended user, then for any root-context process whose parent is an lsws or cpanel plugin binary in the same time window. Also check for new SUID files, /root/.ssh authorized_keys mutations, and unscheduled cron entries.
// cPanel JSON API exploit strings shipped via Linux Syslog agent
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("cpanel_jsonapi_func=generateEcCert", "cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize")
   or SyslogMessage matches regex @"cert_action_entry\s+.*geneccert"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects exploitation attempts against the LiteSpeed cPanel user-end plugin via the generateEcCert / packageUserSize JSON API endpoints used in the UNIX symlink-following privilege escalation chain (CVE-2026-54420, CVE-2026-48172).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-another-actively-exploited-cpanel-plugin-flaw/

  - attack.t1505.003

      - 'cpanel_jsonapi_func=packageUserSize'

Symlink to cPanel/LiteSpeed Root-Owned Paths from Low-Privilege User (CageFS Escape) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the in-jail step of the CVE-2026-54420 chain: a low-privilege CageFS-confined user invoking ln -s to plant a symbolic link targeting /usr/local/lsws, /usr/local/cpanel, or /var/cpanel — the bait the vulnerable plugin then follows back into root-owned space. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact directories the LiteSpeed plugin reads when handling generateEcCert/packageUserSize. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit description of the bug — 'UNIX symlink following weakness' inside the LiteSpeed cPanel plugin escaping CloudLinux/CageFS isolation. The target directories /usr/local/lsws, /usr/local/cpanel, /var/cpanel are the canonical roots the plugin reads when handling the generateEcCert / packageUserSize endpoints UC1 alerts on; a symlink from a jailed user to those paths is the bait the bug follows. Excluding well-known service accounts cuts most operational noise without losing attacker signal.
ATT&CKT1548 T1068 T1222.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WHM/cPanel addon installers (Softaculous, Installatron, RVskin) symlinking templates into /var/cpanel during install
  • Reseller management scripts that link a customer's mailbox templates back into cPanel-owned spool dirs
  • Helpdesk/sysadmin troubleshooting where an operator su's to a customer account and creates a diagnostic symlink
  • cPanel transfer-tool restore operations linking restored backup paths into /var/cpanel
  • Custom plugin authors using ln -s as part of plugin self-registration under /usr/local/cpanel/3rdparty
Suppression filter
// Drop installer-pattern symlinks (Softaculous, Installatron, cPanel transfer tool)
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "ln"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-s"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/usr/local/lsws", "/usr/local/cpanel", "/var/cpanel")
| where AccountName !in~ ("root","cpanel","lsws","nobody","mailnull","cpaneleximscanner")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any ("/usr/local/cpanel/3rdparty/", "/scripts/restorepkg", "/usr/local/cpanel/whostmgr/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("softaculous","installatron","restorepkg","pkgacct")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the cPanel user who ran the ln -s, the exact link path created, and the symlink target. If the user is a real customer account (not a service/admin), and the target is a file the LiteSpeed plugin reads (cert configs, package metadata under those dirs), treat as a likely active exploit. Step 2 (contain): Suspend the customer account, capture the symlink and the link's parent directory for forensics, force LiteSpeed plugin upgrade to 2.4.8+, and audit /etc/passwd, /root/.ssh/authorized_keys, and crontabs for fresh modifications. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate the symlink timestamp ±5 minutes with UC1 access-log hits from the same host, and run UC3 against the same time window to surface any root-context process spawned by lsws/cpanel binaries.
// Low-priv ln -s pointing at cPanel/LiteSpeed root-owned paths
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "ln"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-s"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/usr/local/lsws", "/usr/local/cpanel", "/var/cpanel")
| where AccountName !in~ ("root","cpanel","lsws","nobody","mailnull","cpaneleximscanner")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DvcOs has "Linux"
| where ActingProcessName endswith "/ln" or ActingProcessName == "ln"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-s"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/usr/local/lsws", "/usr/local/cpanel", "/var/cpanel")
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("root","cpanel","lsws","nobody","mailnull","cpaneleximscanner")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Root Shell or Persistence Tool Spawned by lsws/cpanel Plugin Parent (Post-Exploit) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the post-exploitation tell of CVE-2026-54420 / CVE-2026-48172: a root-context shell, scripting interpreter, network tool, or account/key/cron utility whose parent is a binary under /usr/local/lsws/ or /usr/local/cpanel/. Article-specific because successful exploitation of the symlink-following bug yields root via the plugin's own process tree. Rationale: Anchored on the kill-chain Phase 3 detection hint: 'unexpected root-context process spawns parented by lsws/cpanel plugin binaries' — directly derived from the article's CloudLinux/CageFS-to-root escape narrative. The child binary set targets the textbook post-root actions Phase 5 calls out: 'new SUID binaries, cron entries, SSH key additions in /root or other users' ~/.ssh, and modifications to cPanel/WHM configuration files'. lsws and cpanel plugin binaries almost never legitimately fork interactive shells.
ATT&CKT1548 T1068 T1496 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WHM upcp (Update cPanel) running as root and invoking curl/wget for package downloads and chmod/useradd as it provisions
  • cPanel cron-tracker / chkservd spawning sh wrappers around health-check scripts
  • LiteSpeed licence renewal cron spawning curl to license.litespeedtech.com
  • WHM AutoSSL spawning ssh-keygen during account certificate provisioning
  • Admin manually running /scripts/restartsrv_* under WHM which fork bash subprocesses
Suppression filter
// Filter cPanel/LiteSpeed maintenance-update flows
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/usr/local/lsws/", "/usr/local/cpanel/")

| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","perl","python","python3","nc","ncat","socat","curl","wget","chmod","chown","useradd","usermod","passwd","ssh-keygen","crontab")
| where not(FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("license.litespeedtech.com","httpupdate.cpanel.net","securedownloads.cpanel.net","updates.cpanel.net"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("upcp","chkservd","cpkeyclt","autossl_check")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the exact child commandline. curl/wget to known cPanel/LiteSpeed licence/update endpoints (license.litespeedtech.com, httpupdate.cpanel.net, securedownloads.cpanel.net) is almost certainly maintenance; everything else — especially ssh-keygen, useradd, crontab editing /root or another user's crontab, chmod u+s — is presumptive compromise. Cross-reference timestamps with UC1 access-log hits and UC2 symlink-creation events on the same host. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep /etc/cron.d, /etc/crontab, /var/spool/cron, /root/.ssh/authorized_keys, all user ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, and find / -perm -4000 -newer <plugin install marker> across every co-tenant on the affected shared host; assume every co
